findings.headline: Awaab's Law compliance consuming increasing resources through 2027 with Amber delivery status
findings.detail: Mandatory compliance with Awaab's Law (addressing damp, mold and hazards) is consuming progressively more resources, tracked to reach 95% by Q4 2027. Current status is Amber, indicating the council is behind scheduled milestones. Surveys and remedial works are being tracked with escalating resourceing across 2026-27.
findings.matters: Mandatory regulatory compliance requirement consuming significant and increasing budget allocation through 2027; reduces financial flexibility for discretionary spending
findings.figures: Resourceing progression: Q1 80%, Q2 85%, Q3 90%, Q4 95%
findings.quote: Ensure resources and processes are in place to resolve HHSRS actions promptly keeping numbers of non-decent homes at a minimum.

findings.headline: Housing Repairs service demand exceeded operational capacity May-June 2026; additional resourcing required
findings.detail: Housing Repairs performance deteriorated sharply in May-June 2026 due to increased demand exceeding available capacity, resulting in higher wait times and call abandonment. Council is proposing additional temporary capacity, revised operating model, and recruitment to dedicated out-of-hours service to recover performance to targets (87.5% calls answered, 3-minute average wait).
findings.matters: Indicates revenue budget pressure requiring supplementary spending on staffing and resources; suggests council faces wider capacity constraints in delivering services
findings.figures: Performance targets: 87.5% calls answered, average wait time 3 minutes, resident satisfaction 85%+
findings.quote: Performance during May and June 2026 deteriorated due to increased Housing Repairs demand and reduced operational capacity, resulting in higher wait times and call abandonment rates.

findings.headline: Stock condition survey contractor falling behind on accelerated programme; only 29.9% complete by July 2026
findings.detail: Council accelerated stock condition survey targeting May 2027 completion to understand housing stock condition and inform investment strategy. Contractor Ridge is behind plan: end April 2026 showed 21% completion, improving to only 29.9% by mid-July. Contractor has been asked to provide assurance of resource commitment to deliver remaining work.
findings.matters: Delays to understanding stock condition prevent strategic capital investment planning and asset maintenance prioritization; directly impacts future capital spending forecasts
findings.figures: End of April completion 21%; mid-July 2026 completion 29.9%
findings.quote: Ridge are currently behind in the delivery of their accelerated plan.

findings.headline: RSH identified 'serious failing' in health and safety compliance data accuracy
findings.detail: Regulator assessment found limited assurance over accuracy of health and safety compliance data, particularly for lifts, asbestos and fire safety. Internal audits identified issues requiring significant improvement. Council is implementing audit recommendations and commissioning external H&S specialist audits across all key areas (gas, electric, fire, asbestos, lifts, legionella).
findings.matters: Serious audit weakness indicates control failures; remediation will require additional specialist audit spending and may expose council to regulatory action
findings.figures: Limited assurance findings on lifts, asbestos and fire safety compliance
findings.quote: LB Islington provided limited assurance over the accuracy of health and safety compliance data, which we consider a serious failing.

findings.headline: Lift maintenance backlog of 1,000+ overdue remedial actions, with 500+ overdue for over a year
findings.detail: RSH inspection found the council has over 1,000 overdue lift remedial actions in communal buildings, with up to 500 overdue for longer than a year. These are non-safety-critical but represent significant deferred maintenance. Council plans closure by end December 2026 with current contractor and will procure new lift contractor by October 2027. Current delivery status is Amber (behind plan).
findings.matters: Represents a material deferred maintenance liability on council housing stock; significant capital catch-up spending will be required to resolve
findings.figures: 1,000 overdue lift remedial actions, with up to 500 overdue for longer than a year
findings.quote: the council reports having over 1,000 overdue lift remedial actions, with up to 500 overdue for longer than a year.

findings.paper_title: CMT - Joint Board - Executive Report_North London Housing Partnership_July 2026 V2
findings.headline: Funding decisions arrive with late notice requiring rapid multi-council approval for service mobilisation
findings.detail: The paper states the service 'receives instruction of funding often at a late notice' and faces 'more complex governance structure in requiring multi-Council approval for the use of the funding.' Delays in mobilisation create risk of contract notices being issued and services being disrupted or lost.
findings.matters: Tight mobilisation timelines combined with multi-council approval requirements create operational risk of missed deadlines and service gaps.
findings.figures: GLA agreement runs to 31 March 2027; historical pattern of late-notice funding decisions
findings.quote: The service receives instruction of funding often at a late notice and has a more complex governance structure in requiring multi-Council approval for the use of the funding. As such, service mobilisation or renewal needs to be rapid. Delays may result in notice being given on contracts and services could be disrupted and/or lost.

findings.paper_title: CMT - Joint Board - Executive Report_North London Housing Partnership_July 2026 V2
findings.headline: No written agreements govern the six-borough partnership despite £3.6m funding flows and multi-council governance
findings.detail: The North London Housing Partnership comprises Barnet, Camden, Enfield, Haringey, Islington, and Westminster, with Islington as host authority managing all grant funding and procurement. The paper explicitly states 'There are no written agreement governing arrangements between the Council, NCLHP and other involved bodies,' creating undefined responsibility for decision-making and liability.
findings.matters: Absence of written inter-council agreements in a multi-council funding arrangement creates legal and financial exposure if partners dispute costs, performance, or liability.
findings.figures: Six boroughs; £3,610,232 managed by Islington as host
findings.quote: There are no written agreement governing arrangements between the Council, NCLHP and other involved bodies. Although the sub-regional model includes a shared outcomes framework, more legal certainty would be established, about responsibility for decision-making and the basis of liability, if written agreements between participants were introduced.

findings.paper_title: CMT - Joint Board - Executive Report_North London Housing Partnership_July 2026 V2
findings.headline: GLA can terminate £3.6m grant agreement on one month notice, paying only for incurred work
findings.detail: The GLA Ending Homelessness Accelerator funding agreement runs to 31 March 2027 and allows the GLA to 'terminate the Agreement at its sole discretion at any time on one month's notice, with responsibility only to pay un-invoiced amounts of incurred expenditure, not all unpaid Funding.' This creates cash flow uncertainty and service continuity risk.
findings.matters: Sudden termination of major funding would force rapid wind-down of services and trigger the contingent homelessness liability, potentially requiring unbudgeted council spending.
findings.figures: £3,610,232 GLA Ending Homelessness Accelerator Programme fund; termination with one month notice
findings.quote: GLA can terminate the Agreement at its sole discretion at any time on one month's notice, with responsibility only to pay un-invoiced amounts of incurred expenditure, not all unpaid Funding.

findings.paper_title: CMT - Joint Board - Executive Report_North London Housing Partnership_July 2026 V2
findings.headline: Contingent liability: Islington must house homeless people if externally-funded services close
findings.detail: Islington has statutory duties under Housing Act 1996 Part 7 to provide accommodation to homeless individuals. If the six currently grant-funded services (including rough sleeping hub and immigration service) discontinue, the council must provide alternative accommodation. The paper notes there is severe shortage of both temporary and permanent accommodation in Islington and Greater London, making alternative provision expensive or out-of-borough.
findings.matters: Loss of these externally-funded services would force Islington to meet unbudgeted homelessness accommodation costs at potentially high unit cost or out of borough.
findings.figures: Multi-Disciplinary Hub (155 targets), Specialist Immigration Service (240 assessments), six services total funded by £3,610,232 GLA grant
findings.quote: Terminating the services currently funded through the grant may lead to the Council potentially breaching one or more of these duties in respect of any Part 7 applicants unless alternative accommodation can be found. There is a severe shortage of both temporary and permanent accommodation in Islington and in Greater London, and any alternative accommodation solutions sourced could be expensive or out of borough.

findings.headline: Stage 1 housing complaints jumped 37% year-on-year to 93 per 1,000 homes
findings.detail: Complaints at stage 1 rose from 68 per 1,000 homes to 93 per 1,000, putting Islington significantly above the London median of 73 per 1,000 (26% above median). Stage 2 complaints also rose from 17 per 1,000 to 29 per 1,000, putting Islington in the lower quartile.
findings.matters: A sharp rise in complaint volume suggests operational or service quality issues that may require management attention; however, this should be read with Stage 1 response times improving to 87% (upper quartile)
findings.figures: Stage 1: 68 per 1,000 (2024/25) to 93 per 1,000 (2025/26); London median 73 per 1,000
findings.quote: Complaints relative to size of the landlord - stage 1 (per 1000 homes): 68 per 1000 [2024/25], 93 per 1,000 [2025/26]

findings.headline: Homes not meeting the Decent Homes Standard rose from 4% to 9% in one year
findings.detail: Islington's proportion of homes failing to meet the Decent Homes Standard increased significantly from 4% in 2024/25 to 9% in 2025/26, placing the council below the London median of 7% and in the lower middle quartile. This represents either an acceleration of deferred maintenance or a shift in measurement classification.
findings.matters: Councils are required to remediate homes not meeting the Decent Homes Standard; this deterioration signals a capital spending requirement and declining stock condition that lenders would see as a financial pressure
findings.figures: 4% (2024/25) to 9% (2025/26); London median 7%, London upper quartile 4%
findings.quote: Homes that do not meet the Decent Homes Standard: 4% [2024/25], 9% [2025/26]

findings.headline: Tenant Satisfaction Measure reporting failed in 2024/25 due to system issues affecting complaints data, with third-party audit pending to verify correction by 1 March 2027.
findings.detail: Islington did not fully meet Tenant Satisfaction Measure requirements in its 2024/25 information return to the Regulator due to system issues affecting complaints information. Monthly audits of stage 1 complaints and quarterly audits of stage 2 complaints are underway. A third-party audit has been completed with recommendations; internal work to comply is expected by 1 March 2027.
findings.matters: Failure to meet regulatory reporting requirements on tenant satisfaction, combined with system issues in complaints data, suggests data quality problems that could mask service failures. The reliance on third-party verification indicates internal confidence is insufficient.
findings.figures: 2024/25 return failed to meet requirements; third-party audit completion; internal compliance deadline 1 March 2027
findings.quote: Islington Council did not fully meet the Tenant Satisfaction Measure requirements in its 2024/25 information return to the Regulator, due to system issues affecting its complaints information. LB Islington is addressing this issue and plans to seek third-party verification on its information to gain assurance that this weakness has been resolved.

findings.headline: Council committed to £2.426 billion in housing investment over 30 years, with £485 million in next five years, accelerated by regulatory compliance requirements.
findings.detail: The HRA Business Plan, approved February 2026, commits £2.426 billion over 30 years (£485 million over next five years) plus £53 million annually for response repairs. The draft Corporate Plan advances this with £58 million for buyback programme and £388 million to ensure all homes meet Decent Homes Standard by 2030, in response to regulatory findings.
findings.matters: These figures represent material commitments that will shape HRA borrowing and financing for the next five years, driven by regulatory compliance rather than discretionary investment. The scale indicates the council anticipates significant unmet capital needs.
findings.figures: £2.426bn over 30 years; £485m over next 5 years; £53m annually for response repairs; £58m buyback programme; £388m for Decent Homes compliance by 2030
findings.quote: The HRA Business Plan, approved by the Council in February 2026, outlined significant continued investment in the Council's stock. This included: Investing £2.426 billion over the 30-year life of the plan, £485 million of which will be invested over the next five years.

findings.headline: Most of Islington's homes lack formal condition surveys: only 27.2% of internal surveys and 3% of external surveys completed as of June 2026, despite homes being required to meet Decent Homes Standard.
findings.detail: 87% of council homes have condition surveys more than ten years old and lack formal Housing Health and Safety Rating System (HHSRS) assessment. As of 30 June 2026, 7,025 internal surveys (27.2%) and 762 external surveys (3%) had been completed. The council accelerated the main programme completion date from July 2030 to May 2027 following Executive approval on 25 June 2026.
findings.matters: Incomplete condition surveys across 87% of stock means the council lacks assurance of compliance with Decent Homes Standard. The 3-year acceleration to May 2027 indicates urgent capital needs and will require substantial investment, affecting HRA finances and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: 7,025 internal surveys (27.2%) completed; 762 external surveys completed; programme accelerated to May 2027 from July 2030; condition survey coverage increases ~1% per week
findings.quote: Most of Islington Council's homes have a survey that is more than ten years old and do not have a formal Housing Health and Safety Rating System (HHSRS) assessment. As a result, we do not have assurance that LB Islington's homes meet the Decent Homes Standard. 7025 internal surveys (27.2%) as at the end of June 2026 have been completed and 762 external have been completed – all with HHSRS – condition survey coverage increases by around 1% of stock per week on average.

findings.headline: Over 1,000 overdue lift remedial actions, with 500+ outstanding for longer than a year, representing a critical safety backlog.
findings.detail: The Regulator found that while Islington reported only one non-compliant communal lift during inspection, the council has over 1,000 overdue Lifting Equipment Regulation (LOLER) remedial orders, with up to 500 overdue for longer than a year. Additional resources are being secured to complete this work by 31 December 2026.
findings.matters: A multi-year backlog of overdue lift safety work represents a material unquantified liability and safety risk. The need to secure additional resources to address it signals the scale of the maintenance backlog and raises questions about how comprehensively capital needs have been assessed across the entire housing stock.
findings.figures: 1,000+ overdue remedial actions; 500+ overdue for longer than 1 year; completion target 31 December 2026
findings.quote: In relation to passenger lift safety, while LB Islington reported only one non-compliant communal lift during the inspection, the council reports having over 1,000 overdue lift remedial actions, with up to 500 overdue for longer than a year.

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing downgraded Islington to C3 (non-compliant) on 13 May 2026, with six areas of non-compliance requiring immediate correction.
findings.detail: The Regulator conducted a 5-month inspection and found Islington's housing services non-compliant. The council accepted the C3 grading and immediately developed an improvement plan. The regulatory judgment covered directly managed council housing, PFI contractor homes, and 23 Tenant Management Organisations. Monthly monitoring meetings with the Regulator have been established.
findings.matters: A regulatory downgrade signals loss of confidence in the authority's ability to manage social housing. The requirement for monthly monitoring and the council's commitment to achieve C1 status indicate material management reform is underway, which affects service delivery risk and potentially borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: C3 rating issued 13 May 2026; inspection conducted over 5 months
findings.quote: The Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) issued their judgement to the Council on the 13th of May 2026. The grade was a C3 and the Regulatory Judgment is at Appendix 1. The council fully accepted this grading and immediately developed an Improvement Plan to ensure the council became compliant with the regulatory framework and was reassessed as C1 by the Regulator of Social Housing as soon as possible.

findings.headline: Service expenditure (£1.7m) exceeds general fund budget (£1.442m), with the gap dependent on Health and Social Care recharges and exposed to assessment delays
findings.detail: The general fund budget for short breaks in 2026-27 is £1.442m, but actual expenditure is estimated at £1.7m. The council commissions packages jointly funded by Health, with the North Central London ICB recharging Islington annually. Additionally, young people over 18 continue receiving CYP-commissioned packages while awaiting Health and Social Care assessment completion, with H&SC recharging the full cost. The paper states this means CYP 'commissions over and above the net general fund budget available in CYP', creating dependency on recharge income.
findings.matters: A lender would need assurance on cash flow when the service's baseline operating budget is £0.26m short of actual expenditure, relying entirely on external recharges from a different system experiencing known assessment delays.
findings.figures: General fund budget £1.442m; estimated expenditure £1.7m; £0.258m shortfall; framework maximum £1.7m annually for 8 years
findings.quote: The total general fund budget for commissioned short breaks in Children & Young People (CYP) in 2026-27 is £1.442m. However, the total expenditure in 2026-27 is estimated to be approx. £1.7m... It does mean that CYP commissions over and above the net general fund budget available in CYP.

findings.headline: Short breaks spending grew 30% in three years, with provider cost uplifts of 6.5%-20% and demand growth continuing at 9% annually
findings.detail: Expenditure increased from £1.20m in 2022-23 to estimated £1.6m in 2025-26. Providers have secured significant uplifts in response to wage inflation, including 6.5% for multiple group-based providers and 20% for a major provider. Growth is driven by rising numbers of children with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), increasing at 9% per year. The paper notes the council had to make 'material uplifts' to budgets in 2025/26 due to demand growing faster than previous assumptions. The new framework assumes 10% annual growth going forward and relies on efficiency gains to offset demand.
findings.matters: A lender would need confidence that a service growing at 30% but budgeted at 10% can be controlled, especially when providers are demanding rapid cost increases and demand drivers (EHCP growth) show no sign of slowing.
findings.figures: £1.20m (2022-23) to £1.6m (2025-26) = 30%+ growth; 6.5% and 20% provider uplifts; 9% annual EHCP growth; framework capped at £1.7m annually based on assumed 10% growth
findings.quote: Expenditure has been increasing over the last three years from £1.20m in 2022-23 to an estimated £1.6m in 2025-26, an increase of over 30%. Providers have requested – and in several cases received – significant uplifts for 2025/26, including a 6.5% uplift for multiple group-based providers and a specific 20% uplift for a major group-based provider, in response to wage inflation and sustainability pressures. At the same time, unit costs are increasing.

findings.headline: Council retains £1m self-insurance excess per claim, carrying uninsured operational risk
findings.detail: The council maintains a £1m excess on insurance claims as a deliberate policy to reduce premiums and incentivise internal risk management. This means all operational losses below £1m are unabsorbed by the council and reduce available resources.
findings.matters: A £1m uninsured exposure per incident could impact financial resilience if a major incident occurs below that threshold. The council has chosen to carry this risk to manage insurance costs, creating a potential gap in its risk management framework.
findings.figures: £1m excess per claim
findings.quote: the council self-insures the majority of lower-value claims through a £1m excess

findings.headline: Insurance premium costs rising significantly with further increases expected
findings.detail: Insurance costs increased from £1.66m in 2024/25 to £1.82m in 2026/27, a three-year rise of 9.5%. The council is now budgeting £2.0m per annum for the new contract. The paper explicitly states insurance premiums are subject to market volatility and that 'inflationary or market-related uplifts may be required over time'. A contingency of £0.2m per annum is built in, representing 10% of the base cost, to cover expected inflation and market volatility.
findings.matters: Insurance is a non-discretionary, fixed operational cost. Rising costs squeeze other spending priorities. The £0.2m contingency signals the council expects further increases beyond the £2.0m budget, indicating genuine cost uncertainty in a mandatory expense category.
findings.figures: 2024/25: £1,662,845; 2025/26: £1,718,361; 2026/27: £1,821,651; Proposed budget: £2.0m per annum with £0.2m per annum contingency
findings.quote: Historic annual expenditure has risen over the last three years, reflecting wider insurance market pressures and changes in risk pricing. It is therefore prudent to recognise that inflationary or market-related uplifts may be required over time

findings.paper_title: Draft Housing Improvement Plan report_SB amends
findings.headline: £485 million capital investment over next 5 years committed; HRA Business Plan may require update pending survey completion
findings.detail: HRA Business Plan commits £485 million over next 5 years (£2.426 billion over 30 years). Additional commitments include £25-30 million for lift modernisation (2026-2031), £388 million for housing stock improvements, and £58 million buyback programme. Plan may require revision as stock condition survey data becomes available.
findings.matters: Large capital commitments combined with uncertainty about true stock condition and emerging regulatory requirements create affordability risk; potential HRA plan revision may impact borrowing and reserves.
findings.figures: £485 million over next 5 years; £2.426 billion over 30 years; £25-30 million lift programme; £388 million stock improvements; £58 million buyback
findings.quote: Investing £2.426 billion over the 30-year life of the plan, £485 million of which will be invested over the next five years. The findings from the accelerated survey programme will inform future capital programme prioritisation and may require the HRA Business Plan and capital programme to be updated as more complete stock condition, HHSRS and Decent Homes data becomes available.

findings.paper_title: Draft Housing Improvement Plan report_SB amends
findings.headline: Most council homes lack current condition surveys; 73% more than 10 years old without Housing Health and Safety Rating System assessment
findings.detail: Most of the 25,892 tenanted homes have condition surveys older than 10 years and lack formal HHSRS assessment. As of June 2026, only 27.2% (7,025) of internal surveys completed. Regulator cannot assure Decent Homes Standard is met. Council accelerated completion date from July 2030 to May 2027.
findings.matters: Without current condition data, capital investment planning is impaired and the council lacks baseline assurance for Decent Homes Standard compliance; survey completion will determine actual capital need.
findings.figures: 7,025 internal surveys completed (27.2% of stock) as of June 2026; original completion July 2030 moved to May 2027; 762 external surveys completed
findings.quote: Most of the London Borough of Islington's homes have a condition survey that is more than ten years old and do not have a formal Housing Health and Safety Rating System assessment. As a result, the Regulator does not have assurance that Islington's homes meet the Decent Homes Standard.

findings.paper_title: Draft Housing Improvement Plan report_SB amends
findings.headline: Regulator found 'serious failing' in health and safety compliance data; limited assurance on lifts, asbestos, fire safety
findings.detail: The council provides limited assurance over health and safety compliance data accuracy. Recent internal audits on lifts, asbestos, and fire safety have identified significant improvement gaps, with the regulator explicitly calling this a 'serious failing' indicating weak governance.
findings.matters: Poor data assurance over safety-critical areas indicates weak internal controls and potential for hidden liabilities in areas fundamental to landlord responsibility.
findings.figures: Limited assurance audit findings on lifts, asbestos, fire safety; regulator judgment: May 2026
findings.quote: Islington Council provided limited assurance over the accuracy of health and safety compliance data, which the Regulator considers a serious failing. Recent internal audits of health and safety compliance have provided limited assurance over compliance information in relation to lifts, asbestos and fire safety and have identified issues that indicate that significant improvement is needed.

findings.paper_title: Draft Housing Improvement Plan report_SB amends
findings.headline: Over 1,000 overdue lift remedial (LOLER) actions, with 500+ overdue for longer than a year
findings.detail: Despite reporting only one non-compliant lift during the regulator's inspection, the council has accumulated over 1,000 overdue lift remedial actions. Up to 500 of these have been outstanding for more than a year, representing a significant backlog on safety-critical infrastructure.
findings.matters: Large safety backlog on communal lifts exposes tenants to ongoing risk and represents substantial regulatory and liability exposure; remediation will require significant capital resources.
findings.figures: Over 1,000 overdue lift remedial actions; up to 500 overdue for longer than a year
findings.quote: In relation to passenger lift safety, while Islington Council reported only one non-compliant communal lift during the inspection, the council reports having over 1,000 overdue lift remedial actions, with up to 500 overdue for longer than a year.

findings.paper_title: Draft Housing Improvement Plan report_SB amends
findings.headline: Council downgraded to C3 regulatory grade; Regulator of Social Housing identified six non-compliance areas
findings.detail: Islington received a C3 grade from the Regulator of Social Housing on 13 May 2026, down from the expected C1. The inspection identified six material non-compliance areas: condition survey gaps, health and safety data assurance failures, lift safety backlog, tenant data gaps, TSM reporting issues, and complaints accessibility in TMO properties.
findings.matters: A regulatory downgrade indicates material failures in the council's control environment and ability to manage housing services, affecting its credibility and operational risk profile.
findings.figures: C3 grade (issued 13 May 2026); six non-compliance areas identified
findings.quote: The Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) issued their judgement to the Council on the 13th of May 2026. The grade was a C3 and the Regulatory Judgment is at Appendix 1.

findings.paper_title: Committee report Treasury Full Year 2026 LIs
findings.headline: Forecast shows structural gap between optimal borrowing and planned borrowing: liability benchmark £822m by 2028 vs forecast actual borrowing £431m
findings.detail: The liability benchmark (the estimated optimal amount the council should hold in borrowing) is forecast to grow from £361.6m (March 2026) to £822.4m (March 2028). The council's own forecast for actual borrowing shows £443.6m (March 2026) declining to £430.9m (March 2028). This gap of roughly £400m by 2028 means either reserves will be drawn down substantially, capital spending will be further constrained, or the council will need to borrow at an unfavorable point in the future.
findings.matters: This structural divergence indicates that the council's under-borrowing strategy is not sustainable over the forecast period, creating refinancing risk and potential liquidity pressure.
findings.figures: 31.3.28 Liability benchmark £822.405m vs forecast borrowing £430.965m (gap £391.4m)
findings.quote: Loans CFR 31.3.28: 1203.605m, Less balance sheet resources (391.200m), Net loans requirement 812.405m. [Existing borrowing forecast: 430.965m]

findings.paper_title: Committee report Treasury Full Year 2026 LIs
findings.headline: Capital expenditure plan was cut to 40% of forecast; £162m planned borrowing reduced to £57m actual with no explanation
findings.detail: The council had set out to borrow £162.216m to fund capital expenditure in 2025/26. This was revised down to £64.619m 'due to reduction in capital expenditure' (4.12), and the council ultimately borrowed only £57m. The document does not explain why the capital programme was cut so sharply, or whether this reflects financial constraints or reordering of priorities.
findings.matters: A 60% unplanned cut to a council's capital programme signals either financial stress or a material shift in investment strategy. Lenders would want to understand which, and whether future capital plans are also at risk.
findings.figures: Original borrowing plan £162.216m → revised £64.619m → actual £57m. Original capital spend plan reduced by approximately 60%.
findings.quote: The Council set out to externally borrow £162.216m throughout 2025/26. This was reduced to £64.619m due to reduction in capital expenditure. The Council borrowed £57m

findings.headline: Total pension fund underperformed its benchmark across all measurement periods, with value declining £47m in one quarter
findings.detail: Islington's combined pension fund returned 9.3% over the past 12 months versus a benchmark of 11.8%, a 2.5 percentage point shortfall. Over three years it returned 8.7% versus 10.2% benchmark, and over five years 6.2% versus 7.1%. The fund value declined from £2,229.1m at end-2025 to £2,181.8m by end of Q1 2026.
findings.matters: Consistent underperformance across multiple periods indicates the fund's strategic allocation is not delivering expected returns; at the next triennial valuation, this will require the council to increase employer contributions, adding to budget pressure
findings.figures: 12-month underperformance 2.5pp (9.3% vs 11.8%); 3-year underperformance 1.5pp (8.7% vs 10.2%); 5-year underperformance 0.9pp (6.2% vs 7.1%); fund value declined £47.3m in one quarter
findings.quote: Combined LBI fund performance hedged: Period 1 year per annum 9.3%, Customised benchmark 11.8%; 3 years per annum 8.7%, Customised benchmark 10.2%; 5 years per annum 6.2%, Customised benchmark 7.1%

findings.headline: Commercial property fund rent collection fell to 94.4%, signalling tenant financial distress
findings.detail: Columbia Threadneedle's TPEN UK commercial property fund is collecting only 94.4% of rents due. The fund notes it is managing occupiers 'on a case-by-case basis' to agree collection strategies while observing government rent-protection legislation, indicating tenants are experiencing financial difficulty.
findings.matters: Below-full rent collection is an early signal of tenant financial stress and deteriorating commercial property fundamentals; if collection rates continue to fall, property values could decline materially and trigger losses on the fund's portfolio
findings.figures: Rent collection 94.4%; fund value £135m
findings.quote: Rent collection is at 94.4%. TPEN continues to work with its occupiers on a case-by-case basis to agree appropriate strategies for rent collection having regard to government legislation.

findings.headline: Aviva property fund has £62 million in outstanding redemptions approaching a December 2026 deadline
findings.detail: The Aviva UK property portfolio (£190.6m holding) carries £62m in redemption requests that must be met by December 2026. The fund manager sold three properties in Q1 totalling £25m specifically to generate redemption cashflow, but more than half the redemption liability remains outstanding as the deadline approaches.
findings.matters: A firm redemption deadline creates a specific liquidity risk; if the fund manager cannot deliver on schedule, it could force rushed asset sales, impair values, or delay the council's cash receipt and create a cashflow shortfall
findings.figures: Outstanding redemptions £62m; deadline December 2026; three properties sold Q1 for £25m; fund value £190.6m
findings.quote: Three investments were sold over the quarter that has increased cashflow for redemption but has reduced the fund risk of default by 18%. There was £25m new commitments through the secondary market and as such outstanding redemptions now stand at around £62m and the fund has up to December 2026 to deliver.

findings.headline: LCIV RBC equity fund underperformed by 3.7% annually; detailed review results pending as of report date
findings.detail: The LCIV RBC Sustainability Exclusion fund (£219.31m, 10% of total fund) underperformed its annual benchmark by 3.7 percentage points. The report states that a detailed review was completed in April but results remain awaiting as of the July report publication, leaving uncertainty about management action.
findings.matters: Persistent underperformance on the largest equity holding with no reported action creates uncertainty about the fund's strategy and future performance; if the review triggers a management change, it could create transition costs
findings.figures: Annual underperformance -3.7% (portfolio 12.6% vs benchmark 16.3%); quarterly underperformance -3.0%; fund value £219.31m
findings.quote: The fund underperformed its quarterly benchmark to March by -3.0% and a twelve-month under performance of -3.7%. A detailed review was completed in April and awaiting the results.

findings.headline: LCIV Newton equity fund severely underperformed with 12-month deficit of 11.4 percentage points on the second-largest fund holding
findings.detail: Newton, a £332.1m global equity holding (15.2% of the total fund), returned 6.4% over 12 months against a benchmark of 17.9%. The underperformance was caused by deliberate underexposure to energy stocks and weak stock selection in Consumer Staples and Healthcare, where the fund fell behind as those sectors recovered.
findings.matters: This scale of underperformance on a major holding means the council's pension fund is not delivering expected returns, which will flow through to higher employer contributions at the triennial valuation, adding pressure to the council's budget
findings.figures: 12-month underperformance -11.4% (portfolio 6.4% vs benchmark 17.9%); fund value £332.1m; Q1 return -6.1%
findings.quote: The fund returned -6.1% against a benchmark of -1.1% for the March quarter and a 12month under performance of -11.4% against a benchmark of 17.9%. The Sub-fund's lack of exposure to energy stocks was a key underperformance driver, alongside stock selection within Consumer Staples and Healthcare.

findings.headline: Investment management fees jumped 30% to £12.9m from £9.9m, eroding fund returns.
findings.detail: Charges for managing the pension fund portfolio increased from £9.9m to £12.9m. While the council attributes this to higher asset values rather than fee rate increases, the absolute cost is material. Higher fees reduce the net return available to the fund.
findings.matters: Every pound spent on investment management is a pound not available to reduce the contribution burden on the council. A 30% fee increase in one year warrants scrutiny of fee structures and whether passive or lower-cost strategies have been considered.
findings.quote: Investment management fees including charges on pooled funds where fees are deducted at source, on both private and public portfolio are shown in the accounts as £12.9million to give transparency on cost compared to £9.9million in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Employer pension contributions increased to £52.3m, up £4.0m year-on-year due to staff pay awards.
findings.detail: The council's employer contributions to the LGPS scheme rose from £48.3m to £52.3m (8.3% increase). The increase is attributed to pay rises awarded to staff in 2025/26. This is a material and growing claim on the council budget.
findings.matters: Pension contributions are a mandatory cost that competes with service spending and capital investment. Rapid growth signals either widening actuarial deficits or wage inflation feeding directly through to costs.
findings.quote: Employers' contributions including deficit contributions amounted to £52.3million compared to the £48.3million in the previous year. This marginal increase is in part due to the pay increases for staff in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Pension fund operating at a £24.3m annual deficit between contributions received and benefits paid, covered only by investment income.
findings.detail: For the year to March 2026, the fund received £93.5m in income (contributions and transfers) against expenditure of £117.8m (primarily pensions paid). The £24.3m gap was not met by contribution income and required investment returns to cover it. This indicates the fund's contribution base alone is insufficient to meet current benefit obligations.
findings.matters: If investment returns weaken, the council would face pressure to increase employer contributions to close the gap. A sustained market downturn could force material increases to this £52.3m annual cost, crowding out council service spending.
findings.figures: Income £93.5m, expenditure £117.8m, difference £24.3m
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, £93.5million income (excluding investment income) was received against an expenditure of £117.8 million. The shortfall between income and expenditure did not lead to sale of investments because of investment income.

findings.headline: Market volatility after balance sheet date linked to US tariff announcements creates forward return uncertainty
findings.detail: The going concern assessment notes 'significant volatility in markets shortly after the accounting date, in part due to the announcements on tariffs coming from the USA.' The fund's return over the one-year period was marginally below its customised benchmark, and future returns remain subject to macro uncertainty. This could affect the adequacy of contributions if equity returns weaken.
findings.matters: A lender should track whether forward market volatility erodes the fund's 112% funding level — if returns fall short, the council may face contribution rate increases again, requiring budget flexibility that may not exist
findings.figures: Fund valuation increased £170m but performance was marginally below customised benchmark over one year
findings.quote: There was significant volatility in markets shortly after the accounting date, in part due to the announcements on tariffs coming from the USA.

findings.headline: Funding level improved sharply to 112%, eliminating the need for separate deficit recovery contributions
findings.detail: The actuarial valuation at 31 March 2025 showed the fund's assets (£2,038m) represented 112% of past service liabilities (£1,822m), a marked improvement from 96% at the 2022 valuation. This surplus of £217m means the fund no longer requires additional lump sum deficit recovery contributions; instead the council now benefits from a surplus offset of approximately £4m per annum, as the recovery plan has been met.
findings.matters: A funding level of 112% significantly reduces financial risk for the council — the pension scheme is now a asset-positive position rather than a drain, meaning the council is no longer paying additional cash to bridge a gap, improving cashflow sustainability
findings.figures: Funding level 112% at 31 March 2025 (96% at 2022 valuation); surplus £217m; opening net assets £2,038m, closing £2,212m
findings.quote: On the basis of the assumptions adopted, the Fund's assets of £2,038 million represented 112% of the Fund's past service liabilities of £1,822 million (the "Solvency Funding Target") at the valuation date.

findings.headline: Investment management fees increased 30% in one year, from £10.0m to £13.0m
findings.detail: Total management expenses rose 27% from £12.5m to £15.9m, driven primarily by investment management fee increases of 30% (£9.977m to £13.035m). The fund notes fees are 'broadly based on the market value of the investments under their management', meaning the increase reflects both growth in assets and potentially higher fee rates or manager performance adjustments.
findings.matters: For a lender monitoring council efficiency, a 30% jump in investment fees is material — it reduces net returns to members and the fund, and suggests either asset allocation changes toward higher-cost alternatives (private equity/infrastructure) or fee rate increases that should be challenged
findings.figures: Investment management expenses £13.035m (2025/26) vs £9.977m (2024/25); total management expenses £15.858m vs £12.478m
findings.quote: Investment Management Expenses Management Fees 9,939 [2024/25] to 12,996 [2025/26]

findings.headline: Outstanding investment commitments jumped 39% to £164m, creating future cash flow obligations
findings.detail: The fund's undrawn commitments to private equity, property, infrastructure and private debt managers grew from £118m to £164m. The largest commitments are to private debt managers (Churchill £37.9m, LCIV £35.1m, Crescent £6.7m), infrastructure (Pantheon GIF IV £13.5m, LCIV Nature Base £20.8m) and private equity (Clean Growth £12.0m, Pantheon Ventures £4.2m). These represent calls the fund must meet in cash within agreed timescales.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the fund's cash flow commitments; these £164m calls could require the fund to liquidate assets or draw on cash reserves, potentially at unfavourable moments or prices, affecting the council's ability to redirect cash elsewhere
findings.figures: Outstanding commitments £164m at 31 March 2026 (£118m at 31 March 2025); split across private equity (£19.1m), property (£9.2m), infrastructure (£47.6m), private debt (£88.1m)
findings.quote: The Fund has outstanding commitments totalling £164m as at 31 March 2026 (£118m as at 31 March 2025).

findings.headline: Employer pension contribution rate cut from 18.3% to 14.9%, phased over three years from April 2026
findings.detail: The triennial actuarial review (effective 1 April 2026) reduced the employer contribution rate to 14.9% of pensionable payroll, down from 18.3% in 2024/25. The 2025 valuation also moved the fund from deficit recovery contributions to a surplus offset of approximately £4m per annum on average, eliminating the need for separate lump sum deficit recovery payments beyond the agreed 19-year recovery plan.
findings.matters: This is material cost relief for the council's budget — a reduction of around 3.4 percentage points directly reduces pension cost contributions going forward, improving the council's financial sustainability
findings.figures: Primary contribution rate 16.0% (future service); employer normal contribution 14.9% phased over 3 years (from 18.3%); surplus offset approximately £4m per annum
findings.quote: The last review as at 31 March 2025, effective from 1 April 2026 fixed at 14.9% of pensionable payroll costs phased over 3 years (18.3% in 2024/25).

findings.headline: Islington must complete its Investment Management Agreement with London CIV by September 30, 2026 to comply with statutory pooling requirements, but as of July the IMA was still being negotiated.
findings.detail: The Local Government Pension Scheme (Pooling, Management and Investment of Funds) Regulations 2026 require Islington's pension fund to be fully pooled by September 2026. This requires the council to sign an Investment Management Agreement (IMA) with London CIV. As of the July 2026 meeting, officers were 'still discussing the schedules and documentations with LCIV' with multiple schedules outstanding, including portfolio listings, fund objective, target asset allocations, responsible investment policy, and oversight charges. The original expectation was April 1, 2026, but the timeline slipped due to delays in regulations being published.
findings.matters: A lender assesses regulatory compliance risk; a statutory pooling requirement with a hard deadline that remains incomplete three months before deadline creates governance breach exposure and raises questions about council capacity to meet mandatory financial obligations.
findings.figures: September 30, 2026 deadline; original deadline was April 1, 2026
findings.quote: The expectation was that the Council will be required to pool the Fund's assets from 1 April 2026, however because of the delay in the regulations the preparation to pass on the monitoring and oversight is still ongoing and the new timeline being worked to is 30th September.

findings.paper_title: CMT - Joint Board - Executive Procurement Report SH and FS Framework (1)
findings.headline: External grant and NHS funding totalling £3.5m annually (23% of service spend) is assumed to continue despite acknowledged risk of withdrawal
findings.detail: Current annual spend on these services is £15.1m, with £3.5m from external funding (NHS and grants). Section 10.1.5 explicitly states: "there is a risk that some streams particularly external funding may be reduced or withdrawn, which could impact the overall budget envelope." The paper does not detail how the council would absorb this loss from its own budgets if external funding is withdrawn.
findings.matters: Loss of £3.5m external funding would represent a material unfunded cost pressure—23% of service budget—requiring either service reduction or reallocation from other council budgets
findings.figures: £3,487,800 external funding annually (23% of £15,064,336 total spend); council's own contribution £11,576,536
findings.quote: It is assumed that funding will continue in future years, however, there is a risk that some streams particularly external funding may be reduced or withdrawn, which could impact the overall budget envelope.

findings.paper_title: 2526-0430 Procurement Strategy - Domestic Gas Boiler Installation Servicing and Repairs - FINAL 05 06 26 - 12 27
findings.headline: In-house gas team understaffed at 63% capacity, forcing reliance on expensive external contractors.
findings.detail: Section 3.8 states the in-house team is 'currently operating at approximately 63% of its planned staffing capacity' due to 'significant challenges in recruiting and retaining sufficient qualified personnel.' This forces the council to procure expensive external contractors. Section 3.9 notes the council is addressing this through an apprenticeship programme, but this provides only 'two apprenticeship opportunities during the term of the contract' and is described as a 'medium-term mechanism.'
findings.matters: Low in-house capacity means council cannot reduce reliance on expensive subcontractors and therefore cannot control costs through in-sourcing. Planned apprenticeship programme does not address near-term cost pressures, leaving the council dependent on external suppliers for years.
findings.figures: In-house team at 63% staffing; 2 apprentice positions planned; 9 Gas NVQ placement opportunities per annum proposed.
findings.quote: The in-house gas team continues to encounter significant challenges in recruiting and retaining sufficient qualified personnel and is currently operating at approximately 63% of its planned staffing capacity. This shortfall presents a risk to service continuity and compliance with statutory landlord obligations.

findings.paper_title: 2526-0430 Procurement Strategy - Domestic Gas Boiler Installation Servicing and Repairs - FINAL 05 06 26 - 12 27
findings.headline: Council committing to £146.6m gas services contract over seven years with no guaranteed minimum work volumes.
findings.detail: Section 3.27 specifies the framework is valued at '£146,612,343.23 (VAT inc.) based on a maximum contract term of eighty-four (84) months.' However, section 3.32 states: 'There will be no guarantee of volumes of works issued under the framework agreements. Values may decrease if there is any further expansion of the in-house teams during the term of the contracts or for any other reasons.'
findings.matters: Large long-term commitment to a service with uncontrolled demand risk creates financial exposure both ways: if actual demand exceeds forecast, HRA faces budget pressure; if forecast overestimated demand, council has locked into expensive contract with low utilization.
findings.figures: £146,612,343.23 (inc. VAT) over maximum 84 months; forecast based on 2025/26 spend of £11.2m with 4% annual inflation and 5% asset growth applied.
findings.quote: There will be no guarantee of volumes of works issued under the framework agreements. Values may decrease if there is any further expansion of the in-house teams during the term of the contracts or for any other reasons.

findings.paper_title: 2526-0430 Procurement Strategy - Domestic Gas Boiler Installation Servicing and Repairs - FINAL 05 06 26 - 12 27
findings.headline: Gas boiler contracts have exceeded their budgeted values, driven by regulatory obligations and demand factors the council cannot control.
findings.detail: Section 2.3 states 'The current arrangement for domestic gas boiler installations has exceeded its contract value.' Section 3.26 identifies the causes as 'winter spikes in reactive repairs and boiler failure replacements, the unanticipated uplift in demand following the return of PFI2 properties, and an accelerated response to damp and mould cases alongside emerging Awaab's Law expectations and wider regulatory scrutiny.' Lots 2 and 3 are specifically noted as in overspend.
findings.matters: Contract overruns demonstrate the council's cost forecasts are underestimating demand. Regulatory requirements (Awaab's Law, damp/mould compliance, building safety) are driving uncontrollable cost increases the council cannot avoid, making budget planning more difficult.
findings.figures: Gas Lots 2 and 3 combined spending rose from £5.6m (2022/23) to £8.5m (2025/26), a 52% increase in four years.
findings.quote: the reasons for increased spend have largely been service-led and risk-led rather than discretionary. These have included winter spikes in reactive repairs and boiler failure replacements, the unanticipated uplift in demand following the return of PFI2 properties, and an accelerated response to damp and mould cases

findings.paper_title: 2526-0430 Procurement Strategy - Domestic Gas Boiler Installation Servicing and Repairs - FINAL 05 06 26 - 12 27
findings.headline: Subcontractor spending consistently exceeds budget, with council warning that containment is becoming progressively more difficult.
findings.detail: Section 10.1.10 states that 'expenditure on subcontractors has consistently exceeded its allocated budget on an annual basis' and the broader repairs budget 'has managed to mitigate some of the financial pressures' but warns 'the task of keeping expenditure within the existing budget limits is becoming progressively more difficult.' The council explicitly warns that if overruns cannot be contained, they may need to either grow the HRA or 'find savings from major works (capital) or from day-to-day landlord activities such as housing management.'
findings.matters: Inability to control subcontractor spending threatens HRA financial sustainability. If overruns continue and cannot be absorbed by the broader budget, the council faces forced choices between growing HRA debt, cutting capital investment in housing, or reducing housing management services—all of which affect financial health.
findings.figures: Gas services spending: £7.7m (2022/23), £9.0m (2023/24), £10.2m (2024/25), £11.2m (2025/26); revenue servicing budget £2.880m against 2025/26 forecast spend of £3.026m.
findings.quote: In the event expenditure cannot be contained within allocated budgets then any financial pressures would represent growth to the HRA, and it may become necessary to find savings from major works (capital) or from day-to-day landlord activities

findings.paper_title: Contract Variation of Stock Condition Survey Programme EMRB 09.05.26
findings.headline: Energy Performance Certificate assessment capacity gap affecting 18,148 of 25,587 homes (71% outstanding) as of April 2026
findings.detail: The council identified a gap in EPC contract provision and is adding £723,519 to expand capacity. As of 24 April 2026, only 7,439 of 25,587 homes had valid EPCs, leaving a backlog of 18,148 properties. The contractor will take over EPC delivery on an interim basis until a new procurement is initiated. This represents an unmet compliance obligation affecting lettings and Right to Buy sales.
findings.matters: Large backlogs in statutory compliance requirements for lettings and sales indicate operational inefficiency and potential constraints on housing revenue generation.
findings.figures: 18,148 EPCs outstanding of 25,587 homes (71% backlog); £723,519 additional cost; average 900–1,100 homes relet annually; 98 EPCs for RTB in 2024–2025
findings.quote: As of April 24th, 18,148 EPCs out of 25,587 homes remain to be completed.

findings.paper_title: Contract Variation of Stock Condition Survey Programme EMRB 09.05.26
findings.headline: 20-year-old housing asset management system reaching end-of-life, requiring £78,905 additional integration cost mid-programme
findings.detail: The Strategic Asset Management (SAM) system holding all housing stock information is 20 years old, no longer supported by its developer, and will be decommissioned in 2026/27. The council must pay additional £78,905 to configure the NEC Asset Module as a replacement and ensure stock condition survey data integrates correctly. This deferred IT maintenance is now creating cascading costs during a regulatory compliance programme.
findings.matters: Legacy IT systems reaching end-of-life during critical regulatory programmes indicate poor asset management discipline and risk of further unfunded costs.
findings.figures: £78,905 for NEC Asset Module configuration; system decommissioning date 2026/27; system age 20 years
findings.quote: The council's Strategic Asset Management (SAM) IT system is currently used to hold all the asset information about the council's housing stock. It is 20 years old and has reached end-of-life and is no longer supported by its developer; as a result, it will be decommissioned in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Contract Variation of Stock Condition Survey Programme EMRB 09.05.26
findings.headline: Programme acceleration from 5-year to 2-year timeline is non-discretionary regulatory requirement, not operational choice
findings.detail: The survey completion date was originally July 2030 but is now mandated to complete by May 2027 with a mop-up period to 31 August 2027. The council's own management team had decided to accelerate to 2 years, but a further acceleration is now required specifically to comply with the regulator's Consumer Standard. This is not a business-driven timeline but a compliance-driven one.
findings.matters: Non-discretionary regulatory timelines signal the council lacks operational autonomy and is under external control pressure, affecting management credibility and risk profile.
findings.figures: Original completion July 2030; revised completion May 2027; 17 surveyor minimum from May 2026; KPI target 2,040 surveys per month from May 2026
findings.quote: In response to the feedback from the RSH, the main programme completion date is proposed to be brought forward from July 2030 to May 2027, with a mop-up period until 31st August 2027 to cover any stock condition surveys that have not been completed due to difficulties accessing resident's homes.

findings.paper_title: Contract Variation of Stock Condition Survey Programme EMRB 09.05.26
findings.headline: £1.813m HRA budget pressure in 2026/27 funded from reserves to meet regulatory deadline
findings.detail: The council is funding the accelerated survey programme from HRA reserves. The financial impact is heavily front-loaded: £1.813m cost in 2026/27, offset by £0.114m saving in 2027/28 and £0.414m savings in 2028/29 and 2029/30. The HRA holds £17.521m in general reserves, but this represents a material near-term drawdown to meet a regulatory requirement rather than a discretionary investment.
findings.matters: Large, immediate HRA reserve drawdowns for regulatory compliance indicate financial pressure and reduced flexibility for future unexpected costs or service pressures.
findings.figures: 2026/27 cost £1.813m; HRA General Reserves £17.521m; higher unit cost per survey £0.049m in 2026/27; revised profile of surveys £1.050m in 2026/27
findings.quote: It is proposed that this additional cost is funded by HRA reserves. The HRA currently has £17.521m in General Reserves. There is, therefore, sufficient funding available within reserves carried forward to the current financial year to fund the budget required, and cover the additional cost in the first year, to be offset by the savings in the future years.

findings.paper_title: Contract Variation of Stock Condition Survey Programme EMRB 09.05.26
findings.headline: Regulator judgment C3 for serious weakness in housing stock condition assurance — compliance failure driving major cost
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing inspected Islington and downgraded the council to C3 grade specifically due to lack of assurance in stock condition data. The regulator has flagged prompt completion of surveys as critical and can take enforcement action including fines or appointment of new management if standards are not met. This judgment directly triggered the £871,087 contract variation.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance failures signal governance weakness and immediate risk of enforcement action that could impair the council's borrowing capacity and creditworthiness.
findings.figures: C3 grade; £871,087 contract variation; original contract value £1,959,194 (44.46% increase); total variations £982,672 (50% increase when including January 2026 variation)
findings.quote: An inspection of the council by the RSH concluded in a judgement of C3, due to serious weakness in relation to a lack of assurance in our stock condition data because of low levels of survey data being available at the point of inspection.

findings.paper_title: FINAL 2024-26 Q4 performance report (Delivery Plan progress performance update) - tracked. ME edits
findings.headline: Resident satisfaction in some service areas below target, dragging overall score below 85% threshold
findings.detail: Overall resident experience satisfaction fell to below 85% target and rated amber. Access Islington contact centre hit 87% (above target), but satisfaction in other resident experience areas fell below target, pulling the combined score down.
findings.matters: Declining resident satisfaction in non-contact-centre services may indicate service quality issues or rising unmet demand in wider council operations.
findings.figures: Target: 85%; Access Islington achieved 87%; overall combined score: below 85% (amber)
findings.quote: Access Islington (contact centre) satisfaction was 87% above the target, however other residents experience is below target, giving an overall satisfaction rate below the 85% target and thus amber rated

findings.paper_title: FINAL 2024-26 Q4 performance report (Delivery Plan progress performance update) - tracked. ME edits
findings.headline: School surplus capacity remains above healthy benchmark despite downward trend
findings.detail: Surplus capacity in primary and secondary schools remains above the healthy 5–10% benchmark, though trending downward due to closures, amalgamations and reduced admission numbers. This structural oversupply persists.
findings.matters: Persistent school surplus indicates underutilised capital and revenue investments; suggests longer-term estate strategy challenges or demographic headwinds.
findings.figures: Healthy benchmark: 5–10%; actual level not specified but above benchmark
findings.quote: Surplus remains above the healthy 5–10% benchmark but is trending downward

findings.paper_title: FINAL 2024-26 Q4 performance report (Delivery Plan progress performance update) - tracked. ME edits
findings.headline: Emergency hospital admissions rising for residents aged 65+, indicating growing demand pressure on health and social care
findings.detail: Emergency hospital admissions for older residents increased during the year. Partners have identified this as a priority area, with detailed data review underway. This suggests rising acuity and cost pressures in adult social care.
findings.matters: Rising emergency admissions for older people signals either growing need or care coordination gaps, both of which typically drive increased social care expenditure and pressure on council reserves.
findings.figures: No baseline given; described as increased during the year
findings.quote: Emergency hospital admissions for residents aged 65 and over also increased during the year. Partners have already identified this as a priority area for joint improvement work

findings.paper_title: FINAL 2024-26 Q4 performance report (Delivery Plan progress performance update) - tracked. ME edits
findings.headline: Programme paused mid-cycle due to changes in funding position
findings.detail: The Child-Friendly Islington 'Inclusive' activity workstream was paused during Q4 following changes to the funding position. Work shifted to rescoping the pilot to align with revised budget and timeline constraints.
findings.matters: Mid-cycle programme pauses due to funding changes indicate budget variance or cash flow tightness that may constrain other council operations.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Inclusive activity was paused during the quarter following changes to the funding position, and work focused instead on re scoping a viable pilot aligned to programme objectives and timescales

findings.paper_title: FINAL 2024-26 Q4 performance report (Delivery Plan progress performance update) - tracked. ME edits
findings.headline: Housing delivery 18% below target with 31 homes delayed into next year
findings.detail: Completions reached 126 of 154 target, leaving 31 homes subject to unforeseen delays carrying into 2026/27. This represents slippage of approximately 20% against the two-year plan.
findings.matters: Slippage in capital housing delivery indicates either project management challenges or resource constraints, both relevant to financial stability and delivery credibility.
findings.figures: 126 completions against 154 target; 31 homes delayed into 2026/27
findings.quote: The total completions in the period 2024-26 have been 126 against the target of 154 completions. The remaining 31 were subject to unforeseen delays and will be completed in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: FINAL 2024-26 Q4 performance report (Delivery Plan progress performance update) - tracked. ME edits
findings.headline: Cancelled council housing scheme removes 100 homes from pipeline after Finsbury Leisure Centre project abandoned
findings.detail: The council decided not to proceed with the Finsbury Leisure Centre scheme, which accounted for 100 council homes for rent. This forced a material downward revision of the planning consent target from 178 to 78 council homes. The decision removes significant housing delivery capacity.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand capital delivery track record and pipeline stability. Abandoning a 100-home scheme mid-plan signals either financial constraints or project risk.
findings.figures: Target adjusted from 178 to 78 council homes; Finsbury Leisure Centre scheme accounted for 100 council homes for rent
findings.quote: Following the decision not to proceed with Finsbury Leisure Centre (which accounted for 100 council homes for rent) the target for planning consents secured for council homes was adjusted from 178 to 78 council homes

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Housing General Fund REFCUS Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: 2026-27 capital spending of £6.475m forecast with zero capital receipts
findings.detail: The multi-year programme shows planned capital spending of £6.475m in 2026-27 but zero capital receipts are forecast for that year, while capital receipts of £3.168m are forecast in 2025-26 (when spending is only £0.212m) and £43.862m in later years. This timing mismatch means 2026-27 spending must be funded from sources other than capital receipts—either borrowing or reserves—creating a near-term funding dependency.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's capital funding strategy and whether 2026-27 will require additional borrowing or reserve drawdown when receipts are not available, particularly given the council's housing investment is substantial.
findings.figures: 26/27 spending 6.475m, 26/27 receipts £0m; 25/26 spending 0.212m, 25/26 receipts 3.168m; 27/28-34/35 spending 34.821m, receipts 43.862m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Housing General Fund REFCUS Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: Crouch Hall Court scheme shows negative outturn of £51k against £5k budget
findings.detail: The Crouch Hall Court new build scheme had a Q3 revised budget of £5k but actual spending to 31 March 2026 is shown as negative £51k, with forecast outturn also negative £51k. This creates a £56k variance versus budget, which is flagged as requested slippage. This anomalous negative spending requires explanation—either a prior-year reversal, scheme cancellation, or data issue.
findings.matters: Negative outturn on a capital scheme is unusual and signals either a scheme problem, prior-year correction, or data anomaly that a lender needs to understand when assessing capital delivery track record.
findings.figures: Q3 budget 0.005, Q4 actuals (0.051), slippage request (0.056)
findings.quote: Crouch Hall Court - Current New Build: 25/26 Revised Budget at Q3 0.005, Actuals to 31.03.2026 (0.051), Forecast Outturn at Q4 (0.051), Requested Slippage (0.056)

findings.headline: Leaseholder charges income £4.695m above budget
findings.detail: Leaseholder charge income is forecast at £28.038m against budget of £23.343m, a positive variance of £4.695m or 20% above budget. This material variance requires explanation.
findings.matters: A significant leaseholder income variance needs clarification: if from one-off service charge rebalancing it is not sustainable; if structural it improves HRA position but must inform future revenue planning
findings.figures: Budget £23.343m, forecast £28.038m, variance £4.695m above budget
findings.quote: Leaseholder Charges (23.343) (28.038) (4.695)

findings.headline: General Management costs overspend by £7.762m
findings.detail: General management expenditure is forecast at £90.398m against budget of £82.636m, an overspend of £7.762m or 9.4% of budget. This is the largest single expenditure variance and indicates significant operational cost pressures.
findings.matters: A substantial management cost overspend suggests staffing or administrative cost pressures that may be structural, directly affecting HRA sustainability and financial resilience
findings.figures: Budget £82.636m, forecast £90.398m, overspend £7.762m
findings.quote: General Management 82.636 90.398 7.762

findings.headline: Repairs and Maintenance overspend of £5.591m
findings.detail: Repairs and maintenance costs are forecast at £55.981m against a budget of £50.390m, an overspend of £5.591m or 11% of budget. This material variance suggests either higher-than-expected maintenance demand or cost inflation in repair services.
findings.matters: Sustained repairs overspends indicate either deteriorating housing stock requiring increased capital investment, or cost inflation in maintenance that will affect future HRA viability and debt capacity
findings.figures: Budget £50.390m, forecast £55.981m, overspend £5.591m
findings.quote: Repairs and Maintenance 50.390 55.981 5.591

findings.headline: Finsbury Wellbeing Campus and Finsbury Leisure Centre show severe slippage with £2.888m of budgeted investment not delivered by year-end.
findings.detail: Finsbury Leisure Centre: budgeted £1.200m with zero delivered (£1.200m reduction requested). Finsbury Wellbeing Campus: budgeted £1.800m with only £0.112m delivered (£1.688m underspend). Combined, these major wellbeing infrastructure schemes delivered only 4% of planned investment.
findings.matters: Severe slippage on flagship community infrastructure suggests delivery challenges or cost/planning issues that may affect the council's ability to execute capital strategy and could indicate contingencies on other dependent schemes.
findings.figures: Finsbury Leisure Centre £1.200m budgeted, £0 delivered; Finsbury Wellbeing Campus £1.800m budgeted, £0.112m delivered
findings.quote: CWB Finsbury Leisure Centre 1.200 - (1.200) - - - (1.200) - - - ; CWB Finsbury Wellbeing Campus 1.800 0.112 (1.688)

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme is underspending by £15.296m, or 31% of the total £48.761m budget.
findings.detail: Significant slippage across multiple areas: Children's schemes underspent by £3.351m (including £1.356m on High Needs Provision and £0.940m on SEND Mainstream Inclusion); Community Wealth Building underspent by £5.275m; Environment underspent by £6.242m. These represent requested reductions or adjustments rather than delivery delays.
findings.matters: A 31% underspend in capital investment suggests either delivery constraints, cost inflation leading to reprioritisation, or changed strategy; material underspend in SEND and Children's services is particularly relevant given national demand pressures in these areas.
findings.figures: General Fund budget £48.761m, forecast £33.464m, underspend £15.296m (31%)
findings.quote: Environment General Fund Total 48.761 33.464 (15.296)

findings.headline: HRA Property Acquisitions programme has accelerated by £7.970m beyond Q3 revised budget.
findings.detail: The HRA Property Acquisitions scheme budgeted at £70.819m in Q3 is now forecast to spend £78.789m at Q4, representing an overspend of £7.970m (11% increase). This acceleration was requested during Q4.
findings.matters: A significant capital overspend on property acquisitions affects debt capacity and may indicate either higher property costs than assumed or expanded acquisition activity, both relevant to financial sustainability and refinancing assumptions.
findings.figures: £70.819m Q3 budget → £78.789m Q4 forecast, overspend £7.970m
findings.quote: HRA Property Acquisitions 70.819 78.789 7.970 - 7.970

findings.headline: Interest payments underspent by £6.511m due to lower rates, offset by £4.316m MRR top-up
findings.detail: Interest Payments and income underspent by £6.511m, likely due to lower prevailing interest rates or reduced borrowing. However, this saving is partially used to fund a £4.316m top-up to the Major Repairs Reserve due to lower interest payable, suggesting interest savings are being swept into reserves rather than improving the account.
findings.matters: HRA borrowing is the largest component of council debt; sustained interest savings improve viability, but if they are non-recurring due to rate falls, the HRA budget baseline needs resetting to avoid future overspends
findings.figures: £6.511m interest underspend; £4.316m MRR top-up
findings.quote: Interest Underspend Interest Payments and income (6.511) ... Reserves Overspend MRR top up due to lower interest payable 4.316

findings.headline: Bad debt provision increased by £0.474m in Q4
findings.detail: Bad Debt Provision shows a £0.474m overspend for rents and service charge bad debts. This means the council is increasing its provision for uncollectable rents and charges, suggesting collection performance is weaker than budgeted.
findings.matters: Bad debt in the HRA is a cash-flow risk; rising provisions indicate collection issues that reduce the HRA's net income and may signal tenant financial stress
findings.figures: £0.474m overspend
findings.quote: Bad Debt Provision Overspend Bad debt provision for rents and service charge 0.474

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs up £1.283m in Q4
findings.detail: General Management shows a £1.283m overspend on temporary accommodation in the quarter. This represents unbudgeted demand or cost pressure in a discretionary service area.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a cost pressure driven by homelessness and housing shortage; sustained overspends indicate demand the council cannot absorb, affecting reserves and HRA sustainability
findings.figures: £1.283m overspend
findings.quote: General Management Overspend Temporary accommodation 1.283

findings.headline: Disrepair-related costs overrun by £3.786m in Q4, the largest single variance
findings.detail: General Management shows a £3.786m overspend for disrepair costs in the quarter. This is the single largest variance in the HRA and suggests actual repair and maintenance expenditure is materially above budget. The council may be facing a housing stock condition issue or backlog.
findings.matters: HRA viability depends on managing repair costs; a persistent overspend of this scale signals either budget setting problems or deteriorating stock, both material to lending risk
findings.figures: £3.786m overspend
findings.quote: General Management Overspend Disrepair related cost 3.786

findings.headline: Building safety legislation could increase future compliance costs on HRA housing stock
findings.detail: The council notes that legislation changes in relation to building safety could increase the cost of compliance-related works, and there are ongoing government consultations on decent home standards for social housing.
findings.matters: This represents an unquantified future liability that could add to cost pressures already visible in the current repairs and maintenance backlog.
findings.figures: No figures given; unfunded future risk
findings.quote: Legislation changes in relation to building safety could increase the cost of compliance related works to HRA stock. There are also currently government consultations on decent home standards for social housing.

findings.headline: £6.296m in new build feasibility costs could not be capitalised and had to be expensed
findings.detail: Capital project expenditure of £6.296m for new build feasibility works could not be capitalised as assets. A reserve was established in the previous year specifically to absorb this cost, which was fully drawn down.
findings.matters: This shows capital programme challenges: projected asset-creating costs became non-recoverable expenses, requiring pre-positioned reserves and indicating the programme is not delivering as planned.
findings.figures: +£6.296m in non-capitalisable costs (movement of £2.888m worsening from Q3)
findings.quote: There were costs of +£6.296m in relation to capital projects that could not be capitalised for new build feasibility works, a movement of +£2.888m from Q3. A reserve was established in the previous financial year to cover this cost.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend of £1.284m caused by tenant decants during repair works
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation cost £1.284m more than budget because repair works require tenants to be temporarily housed. The council had approximately 30 decant cases in place at year-end.
findings.matters: This is a downstream cost of the repairs backlog: the true cost of the repair program is the repairs budget plus temp accommodation costs, indicating the actual repair delivery rate is unsustainable.
findings.figures: +£1.284m overspend (increase of £0.168m from Q3); around 30 decant cases at year-end
findings.quote: These pressures have also contributed to an overspend of £1.284m within Temporary Accommodation, an increase of £0.168m from Quarter 3, as some repair works require tenants to be decanted, with around 30 cases in place at year-end.

findings.headline: Repairs and maintenance overspend of £1.118m driven by inflationary contractor cost pressures
findings.detail: Repairs and maintenance overspent by £1.118m despite lower winter demand. The council reports 'Demand for repairs remains high, with increased job volumes and ongoing inflationary pressures on contractor costs' and is procuring new contracts to reduce overspends going forward.
findings.matters: Structural cost inflation in repairs that persists despite efforts to contain it signals underlying challenges in managing HRA delivery and cost control.
findings.figures: +£1.118m overspend (reduction of £0.631m from Q3 only due to seasonal demand)
findings.quote: Repairs and maintenance had an overspend of +£1.118m, a reduction of -£0.631 from Q3 due to lower demand over the winter period than initially forecast. Demand for repairs remains high, with increased job volumes and ongoing inflationary pressures on contractor costs.

findings.headline: Housing disrepair claims overspend of £3.786m with sustained case volumes repeating prior year
findings.detail: Disrepair claims overspent by £3.786m. The council reports 'sustained levels of disrepair cases, which remain consistent with the same period last year' and has deployed additional resources to reduce per-case costs and improve resolution timing.
findings.matters: A persistent structural cost in the HRA that repeats year on year indicates stock condition issues and repair backlog that are not being resolved, creating ongoing financial pressure.
findings.figures: +£3.786m overspend (increase of £0.351m from Q3)
