findings.headline: Discretionary fee increase of 3.7% framed as necessary to avoid service reductions due to funding pressures
findings.detail: The council proposes to increase discretionary fees and charges by 3.7% from 1 January 2026 for the 2026-27 financial year to sustain essential services and support the ability to set a balanced budget. The EQIA explicitly states that these increases help reduce the risk of service reductions that would otherwise occur due to funding pressures. The council operates across multiple service areas including parking, housing needs, greenspace and leisure, and planning.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council has structural funding shortfalls and must rely on discretionary fee income to maintain service levels and avoid cuts. This indicates underlying financial stress requiring active mitigation.

findings.matters: High disrepair and damp costs indicate housing stock quality problems that affect rent collection, tenant retention, and may reflect unfunded long-term maintenance liabilities. A lender needs to know if this is a one-time spike or a systemic funding gap.

findings.matters: Regulatory cost changes are outside the council's control but will materially affect HRA viability. A lender needs to know the scale of potential exposure from these changes and whether the council has a plan to fund them.

findings.matters: Reserves are not infinite. A lender needs to know whether the council is managing a temporary pressure or whether it is drawing down reserves to fund an ongoing structural deficit. findings.headline: £0.588m of planned savings marked undeliverable; £1.875m delayed
findings.detail: The council has already identified £0.588m of savings that will not be delivered and £1.875m that will be delayed. The FutureWork Programme (office space release) totalling £1.253m is entirely delayed. Town Centre Management (£0.100m) shows £0.050m undeliverable.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's budget assumptions are holding up. Undeliverable and delayed savings at Q2 suggest either the savings plan was overambitious or that delivery is facing material obstacles.
findings.figures: Undeliverable savings: £0.588m; Delayed savings: £1.875m; FutureWork Programme delayed in full: £1.253m

findings.headline: Social care savings offset by variances; Home Care Recovery and Supporting People Services underperforming
findings.detail: Health & Social Care savings are being offset by variances. Home Care Recovery Model (£0.563m target) has £0.079m offset by variances. Supporting People Services (£0.250m target) has £0.182m offset by variances. Introduction of charging for Assistive Technology (£0.125m target) has £0.091m offset. These suggest either demand pressures or lower take-up of charged services than assumed.
findings.matters: Social care demand pressures are a material risk to local government finances. When planned efficiencies and charging initiatives are offset by variances, it signals demand is not responding as assumed, or service users cannot absorb new charges.
findings.figures: Home Care Recovery Model: £0.079m offset; Supporting People Services: £0.182m offset; Assistive Technology charging: £0.091m offset
findings.quote: Home Care Recovery Model: Implement a 7-day model to reduce ongoing care demand. [and] Introduction of charging for use of Assistive Technology

findings.headline: Environmental and parking enforcement savings delayed or undeliverable; contractor underperformance
findings.detail: Multiple specific savings are not being delivered as planned. Additional enforcement operations (littering and environmental) show only £0.120m delivered against a £0.358m target, with the note that the contractor delivered only £0.120m in 2024/25. Extended parking zone hours (£0.394m) and controllable parking hours (£0.120m) are offset by variances, suggesting demand is lower than assumed or other pressures are emerging. Park gate locking (£0.100m) is offset by variances.
findings.matters: Income-based savings (from enforcement and charging) are often volatile because they depend on public behavior and compliance. When they underdeliver, the council either misestimated demand or faces a serviceability issue. A lender should track whether this is a one-off or a pattern.
findings.figures: Additional enforcement: target £0.358m, delivered £0.120m; Extended CPZ hours: £0.394m offset by variances; Controllable parking hours: £0.120m offset by variances; Park gate locking: £0.100m offset
findings.quote: Additional enforcement operations to increase the level of littering enforcement and other environmental enforcement. Contractor only delivered 120k saving in 24/25.

findings.headline: Digital Transformation requires ongoing revenue budget reallocation and reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The council is funding Digital Transformation through a combination of reserve drawdown and reallocating ongoing revenue budget. A £2.813m virement transfers budget from reserves into Resources to fund Digital Transformation on a continuing basis, rather than treating it as a one-time project.
findings.matters: Reserves are a buffer against unexpected costs. Drawing reserves to fund ongoing operational spending (even if it is IT modernization) reduces financial flexibility. A lender should understand the reserve position and the duration of this commitment.
findings.figures: £2.813m virement to provide ongoing revenue budget for Digital Transformation; Corporate budgets include £2.813m transfer to reserves for Digital Transformation offsets
findings.quote: A virement for £2.813m is proposed to adjust budgets between Resources and Corporate Items to fund Digital Transformation. The Corporate budgets include £2.813m transfer to reserves to help offset reserves drawdowns for Digital Transformation.

findings.headline: Capital projects creating unbudgeted revenue cost pressure requiring £0.642m virement
findings.detail: The council has encountered unbudgeted revenue costs arising from capital projects that were not anticipated when budgets were set. A virement of £0.642m reallocates corporate contingency to Environment & Climate Change to cover these costs on an ongoing basis.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted capital-to-revenue leakage is a sign of weak project governance or changing project scope. A lender needs to know whether this is isolated or part of a pattern, and whether capital project assumptions are sound.
findings.figures: £0.642m virement for unbudgeted capital revenue impacts
findings.quote: A £0.642m virement is requested to adjust Environment & Climate Change budgets for unbudgeted capital impact on revenue costs.

findings.headline: Energy cost contingency depleted; £1.202m reallocation needed to fund ongoing energy pressures
findings.detail: The council created contingency for energy costs when prices were uncertain, but that contingency is now being consumed by actual energy pressures. A virement reallocates £1.202m (£0.895m to Community Wealth Building and £0.307m to Environment & Climate Change) from corporate contingency to fund energy costs on an ongoing basis. This is not a one-off pressure but a structural increase in what the council needs to spend on energy.
findings.matters: Energy cost pressures are material to operating budgets and may persist. A lender should understand whether this is temporary (post-price-spike normalization) or structural (higher baseline for the medium term).
findings.figures: £1.202m virement; £0.895m to Community Wealth Building; £0.307m to Environment & Climate Change
findings.quote: A £1.202m virement is proposed to adjust the budgets between Environment & Climate Change, Community Wealth Building and Corporate Items to re-align energy budgets. Contingency for energy costs was created at a time when there was greater uncertainty over electricity and gas prices. Contingency has been used to fund energy cost pressures where they arose.

findings.headline: Only 60% of planned savings are on track; £4.6m offset by other variances masking budget pressure
findings.detail: Of £17.632m total planned savings, only £10.558m are on track to deliver. A further £4.590m are already being offset by variances in other parts of the budget, meaning the council is experiencing cost pressures that are eating into the savings it needs. This is Q2 of the year, so there is limited time to address shortfalls.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's budget plan is realistic. When a third of planned savings are offset by variances this early in the year, it signals either that the savings assumptions were weak or that unexpected costs have emerged.
findings.figures: Total Savings £17.632m; On track £10.558m (59.9%); Offset by other variances £4.590m (26%)

findings.headline: FutureWork property savings delayed by £1.268m
findings.detail: FutureWork savings of £1.268m (with £1.184m from prior years) are delayed. Alternative proposals for the Laycock building and Newington Barrow Way redevelopment will enable delivery in full by 2027/28, representing significant delay from original schedule.
findings.matters: Delayed savings indicate execution risk on council property strategy and may require accelerated delivery in later years or alternative mitigations.
findings.figures: FutureWork savings delayed £1.268m (£1.184m from prior years)
findings.quote: There is a delay to the delivery of £1.268m of FutureWork savings (£1,184m relate to prior years planned delivery).

findings.headline: Contact centre consolidation savings delivery remains at risk
findings.detail: Of £0.788m contact centre consolidation savings, only £0.435m is forecast to be delivered in 2025/26 while £0.353m is delayed. The council explicitly states this delivery remains at risk because it depends on benefits realisation through channel shift and failure demand reduction.
findings.matters: Savings targets at risk expose the council to larger-than-forecast deficits if transformation benefits do not materialise as planned.
findings.figures: Total contact centre consolidation saving £0.788m; forecast delivery £0.435m; delayed £0.353m
findings.quote: However, the delivery of the £0.435m remains at risk as it is dependent on benefits realisation through channel shift and failure demand reduction.

findings.headline: Planning income structural collapse with service reliant on volatile external funding
findings.detail: Planning income is forecast to be £1.110m below budget due to continued activity downturn affecting planning fees and CIL income. The service's near total reliance on external funding makes it highly sensitive to income changes with limited mitigations available.
findings.matters: A service entirely dependent on volatile external funding represents structural financial risk, particularly if planning activity remains depressed.
findings.figures: Planning income pressure £1.110m; income expected to return to historic levels from 2027/28
findings.quote: Planning income - there is a +£1.110m forecast planning income pressure due to a continued downturn in planning activity affecting planning fees, planning performance agreements, design review panel income and CIL income. The service's near total reliance on external funding makes it very sensitive to income changes.

findings.headline: School balances projected to fall into net deficit in 2026/27
findings.detail: School balances forecast to reach only £1.663m net surplus at end of 2025/26 before falling into deficit in 2026/27. Currently 14 schools are in deficit and 34 in surplus. Decline reflects falling pupil rolls, increasing costs and funding not keeping pace with inflation.
findings.matters: Deficit school balances indicate financial instability and may require council intervention, signalling structural issues in school funding sustainability.
findings.figures: School balances: £5.293m net surplus (end 2024/25), projected £1.663m (end 2025/26), then deficit in 2026/27; 14 schools in deficit, 34 in surplus
findings.quote: School balances have been in decline since 2019/20 primarily due to falling pupil rolls, increasing costs and funding which has not kept pace with inflation.

findings.headline: Pay award creates £1.096m recurrent pressure extending into 2026/27
findings.detail: The actual 3.2% local government pay award exceeded the 2.5% assumption in budget setting, creating a £1.096m pressure. This is explicitly noted as recurrent and must be factored into 2026/27 budget setting.
findings.matters: A recurrent pressure that extends into future financial years indicates reduced flexibility for 2026/27 budget and may require additional savings or income.
findings.figures: Pay award 3.2% vs 2.5% budgeted; recurrent pressure £1.096m
findings.quote: A 3.2% pay award creates an estimated pressure of £1.096m based on the latest calculation. This is a recurrent pressure that would need to be factored into 2026/27 budget setting.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation faces structural pressures with no prospect of relief
findings.detail: TA costs are creating sustained financial pressure with bad debt overspend of £0.701m, prevention spend of £0.348m, and nightly rates rising 12% in 2025/26. The council explicitly states there are no signs locally or nationally that cost pressures will abate.
findings.matters: A structural problem with no mitigation in sight will continue to drain resources and affect the council's ability to balance budgets in future years.
findings.figures: TA overspend £0.100m; bad debts overspend £0.701m; prevention costs £0.348m; nightly rate inflation 12% in 2025/26; case growth 31%
findings.quote: Pressures in TA reflect long-term structural problems with the cost-of-living crisis and housing crisis, it is likely that the financial pressure will remain for the medium term.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block faces mandatory Deficit Management Plan
findings.detail: The High Needs Block has a projected in-year overspend of £2.751m with DSG reserves falling from £3.909m to £0.914m by year-end. EHCP numbers are growing at 9% per year while funding grows at only 3% per year. The DfE requires councils to develop a Deficit Management Plan when DSG surplus has reduced substantially.
findings.matters: A mandatory DMP signals structural imbalance between demand and funding, requiring stakeholder consultation and strategic planning that constrains future financial flexibility.
findings.figures: HNB in-year overspend £2.751m; DSG reserves £3.909m (opening) to £0.914m (closing); EHCP growth 9% per year vs funding growth 3% per year; London Councils estimates £500m combined deficit across all London boroughs
findings.quote: Due to the continued increase in the number of children with EHCPs, estimated growth in placement costs and some uncertainties around placement costs for the new academic year, particularly for post-16 provision, there is a risk that the position reported above will worsen and the HNB will fall into a net deficit in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Individual school balances in decline with 14 schools in deficit; DSG pressure from High Needs Block growth
findings.detail: School balances declined to £5.293m at end 2024/25 with 14 schools in deficit. Forecast to recover to net surplus of £1.663m by end 2025/26. However, 'the primary financial pressure for the DSG remains within the High Needs Block and the continued decline in pupil numbers which is anticipated to impact the expected levels of income.'
findings.matters: Individual school deficits and DSG pressure from High Needs Block reflect structural mismatch between declining baseline pupil numbers and growing SEND demand, creating ongoing budget allocation challenges.
findings.figures: School balances £5.293m end 2024/25; 14 schools in deficit; forecast surplus £1.663m
findings.quote: Individual school balances in Islington have been in decline and balances stood at £5.293m at the end of 2024/25 with 14 schools being in deficit. The primary financial pressure for the DSG remains within the High Needs Block and the continued decline in pupil numbers which is anticipated to impact the expected levels of income.

findings.headline: Interest payable forecast at £3.000m against budget of £10.483m, indicating lower actual borrowing than planned
findings.detail: Corporate items show £5.576m underspend on interest payable due to 'lower borrowing requirement and higher interest rates' contributing to additional interest income. The forecast of £3.000m is only 29% of the £10.483m budget, suggesting significant capital schemes or borrowing plans were not executed.
findings.matters: Substantial variance between budgeted and actual interest costs indicates either deferred capital spending or conservative borrowing assumptions—critical for understanding actual debt position versus medium-term plan.
findings.figures: Interest payable budget £10.483m; forecast £3.000m; variance £5.576m underspend
findings.quote: This includes a -£5.576m underspend on interest payable, as the forecast for the year is £3.000m against a budget of £10.483m. The lower borrowing requirement and higher interest rates have also contributed to additional interest income.

findings.headline: SEND transport overspend of £0.617m from continuing growth in numbers and rising unit costs
findings.detail: SEND Transport is forecasting £0.617m overspend 'due to the continued growth in the numbers of young people requiring transport and the rising costs to meet increased demand.' Mitigations include personal transport budgets, independent travel training, route optimisation, and contract reviews, but demand-led nature limits control.
findings.matters: Rising SEND transport costs reflect growing special needs provision that is demand-led and cannot be easily constrained, indicating structural budget pressure that is likely to persist across medium term.
findings.figures: SEND transport overspend £0.617m
findings.quote: SEND Transport is forecasting a +£0.617m overspend due to the continued growth in the numbers of young people requiring transport and the rising costs to meet increased demand.

findings.headline: £0.588m of savings target (3% of £17.632m total) now assessed as undeliverable, with 11% delayed
findings.detail: Of £17.632m in agreed savings for 2025/26, only 86% (£10.558m) is on track to deliver. A further 11% (£1.875m) is expected to be delayed to future years and 3% (£0.588m) is likely to remain undeliverable. The council states it is 'working to assess whether these are delayed or unachievable' with 'mitigation plans will be developed' for future cycles.
findings.matters: Savings delivery shortfalls indicate either optimistic budget assumptions or service pressures preventing planned efficiencies, with undelivered savings feeding directly into future year deficits if not recovered elsewhere.
findings.figures: Total savings £17.632m; on track £10.558m (86%); delayed £1.875m (11%); undeliverable £0.588m (3%)
findings.quote: Of this, 86% (£10.558m) is currently on track to be delivered in-year or expected to be offset by other variances within services (£4.590m). A further 11% (-£1.875m) is expected to be delayed to future years and 3% (£-0.588m) is likely to remain undelivered.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation bad debt write-offs of £0.701m, with numbers still growing at 27 cases per month
findings.detail: While direct temporary accommodation costs are only £0.100m overspend, 'the most significant pressures are from indirect costs, particularly bad debts, write-offs, and prevention payments, with bad debt and rent arrears alone forecast to overspend by +£0.701m.' Numbers continue to increase though 'at a slower rate than last year (average 27 new cases per month compared to 33 last year)'.
findings.matters: Growing bad debt in temporary accommodation indicates collection challenges or resident inability to pay, creating ongoing exposure that cannot be recovered while demand continues to rise.
findings.figures: Bad debt and rent arrears overspend £0.701m; new cases 27 per month; direct overspend £0.100m
findings.quote: However, the most significant pressures are from indirect costs, particularly bad debts, write-offs, and prevention payments, with bad debt and rent arrears alone forecast to overspend by +£0.701m.

findings.headline: Multiple income streams declining: planning down £1.110m, parking down £0.992m, commercial property down £1.156m
findings.detail: Planning income shortfall is attributed to 'continued downturn in planning activity affecting fees, agreements, and CIL income, which also poses a wider funding risk'. Parking income is down across Pay & Display, suspensions, permits, and road closures. Commercial property income has fallen due to 'reduced rent roll and lease terminations'.
findings.matters: Structural decline across discretionary and property-based income streams suggests ongoing funding pressure unlikely to recover quickly, with cumulative impact of £3.258m creating persistent budget gaps for future years.
findings.figures: Planning income shortfall £1.110m; parking £0.992m; commercial property £1.156m; total £3.258m
findings.quote: continued downturn in planning activity affecting fees, agreements, and CIL income, which also poses a wider funding risk

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account in £2.477m deficit, driven by £3.840m disrepair claims and £3.408m new build feasibility costs
findings.detail: The HRA is forecast to be in deficit by £2.477m at year end, to be covered by reserve drawdown. The largest pressures are £3.840m for 'elevated levels of housing disrepair claims which require additional resources' and £3.408m for new build feasibility costs. Additional pressures from repairs (£2.009m), staffing (£1.997m), and damp/mould (£0.587m).
findings.matters: Significant HRA deficit and reserve drawdown signals systemic housing stock condition issues and construction liability that cannot continue indefinitely, reducing financial headroom and indicating potential future capital requirements.
findings.figures: HRA deficit £2.477m; disrepair £3.840m; new build feasibility £3.408m; repairs £2.009m; staffing £1.997m
findings.quote: The forecast position for the HRA is an in-year deficit of £2.477m. As the HRA is a ringfenced account, any deficit at the end of the financial year will be transferred from HRA reserves.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Capital Budget Monitoring Report, Quarter 2 2025-26
findings.headline: General Fund capital programme forecasting £0.312m overspend at Q2, driven by building regulation changes
findings.detail: Automated Public Toilets scheme (£0.166m) forecasting overspend due to changes in building regulations requiring updated designs and extra ground works at one site. Programme to complete Q3 with management actions to contain overspend, but illustrates cost control risk on design-dependent schemes.
findings.matters: Small overspend signal that scope and cost assumptions embedded in the capital plan are vulnerable to regulatory change or site conditions, relevant to lender assessment of project delivery risk.
findings.figures: £0.312m General Fund overspend; Automated Public Toilets £0.166m contribution
findings.quote: Due to changes in building regulations requiring updated designs, and extra ground works required at one site the programme is forecasting an overspend. The programme will be completed during Q3 and management actions will be taken to manage the overspend.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Capital Budget Monitoring Report, Quarter 2 2025-26
findings.headline: Risk to 2030 decarbonisation target: insufficient capital funding identified
findings.detail: Council identifies explicit risk to corporate priority to decarbonise all corporate buildings by 2030 due to lack of available capital funding. Mitigation proposed is to explore external funding, but no committed solution is named.
findings.matters: Unable capital funding for a named corporate priority signals either constrained overall capital envelope or competing demands. Decarbonisation delays risk regulatory/reputational exposure and may indicate broader capital constraints affecting other priorities.
findings.figures: No budget figures provided; risk identified but unfunded
findings.quote: There is a risk to the council's delivery of the corporate priority to decarbonise all corporate buildings by 2030 due to a lack of available capital funding.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Capital Budget Monitoring Report, Quarter 2 2025-26
findings.headline: Construction inflation forecast at 14% over five years, threatening project viability and forcing scope cuts or additional borrowing
findings.detail: BCIS predicts building costs will increase 14% to 2030. National Living Wage forecast to increase 16% over same period. Council explicitly states cost pressures are "causing costs of projects to increase and risking the financial viability and business cases to projects no longer holding," leaving it to choose between higher budgets (requiring borrowing at 4% Bank Rate) or reduced scope.
findings.matters: Cost inflation without offsetting funding forces a borrowing decision or scope reduction across major programmes. High interest rates (4% Bank Rate) mean additional borrowing adds material revenue costs to MTFS, directly impacting financial sustainability.
findings.figures: BCIS: 14% building cost increase to 2030; National Living Wage: 16% increase forecast to 2030; Bank Rate: 4% (October 2025)
findings.quote: These unavoidable price rises are causing costs of projects to increase and risking the financial viability and business cases to projects no longer holding. This leaves the council in a position of needing to increase budgets to continue to deliver projects as initially planned, or to review scope and adjust the project plans to deliver to the originally agreed budget.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Capital Budget Monitoring Report, Quarter 2 2025-26
findings.headline: Fire safety and lift replacement works (£13.835m combined) delayed by Building Safety Regulator approvals
findings.detail: Fire Safety (£8.595m) and Lifts (£5.240m) programmes for HRA stock report ongoing delays waiting for external Building Safety Regulator to approve applications. Tall Blocks safety investment (£3.989m) similarly impacted. Works are progressing but regulator bottleneck is material.
findings.matters: Delays on fire safety and lift maintenance for council housing stock create both regulatory compliance risk and potential resident safety implications, with knock-on impact on HRA financial stability if remedial work accelerates.
findings.figures: Fire Safety £8.595m, Lifts £5.240m, Tall Blocks £3.989m
findings.quote: Works are progressing but are impacted by delays with the external Building Safety Regulator approving applications.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Capital Budget Monitoring Report, Quarter 2 2025-26
findings.headline: Harvist Estate 24-unit housing scheme paused indefinitely following contractor administration, delaying social rent delivery
findings.detail: The £0.899m scheme to deliver 24 new social rent homes has been paused with no clear restart date. The project plan is being revised and a planning application is expected this year, with return to site not anticipated until next financial year at the earliest.
findings.matters: Indefinite pause on significant housing delivery directly impacts council's ability to manage temporary accommodation pressures and homelessness, a key lever in local government financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £0.899m scheme, 24 units at social rent, £5.012m of budget slipped to future years
findings.quote: The project has been paused due to the contractor falling into administration. The project plan is now being revised with a planning application expected to be submitted this year, allowing a return to site next financial year.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Capital Budget Monitoring Report, Quarter 2 2025-26
findings.headline: Nearly half (44%) of the 2025/26 capital budget is being reprofiled to future years due to widespread delivery delays
findings.detail: At Q2, requested slippage totals £139.488m, equivalent to 44% of the 2025/26 capital budget. This includes delays across transport (People Friendly Streets, Vehicle Fleet Electrification), environment (Bunhill Heat Networks, Air Quality, Cycle Schemes), and housing schemes. Reasons cited include project delays pending review and contractor issues.
findings.matters: Persistent large-scale slippage indicates material execution risk and signals potential delays in delivering housing, transport, and decarbonisation commitments that lenders and executives depend on for financial planning.
findings.figures: £139.488m total slippage (44% of 2025/26 budget); Q2 alone: £39.835m across General Fund (£8.816m) and HRA (£31.019m)
findings.quote: At Q2, the requested slippage from 2025/26 is £39.835m, split between £8.816m General Fund and £31.019m HRA. This brings the total slippage requested during 2025/26 to £139.488m, equivalent to 44% of the 2025/26 capital budget as at 2024/25 outturn.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Housing Repairs and Maintenance Policy 2025
findings.headline: Housing service adopts zero-tolerance damp-and-mould approach with proactive inspection replacing previous reactive model
findings.detail: Policy explicitly shifts from reactive to proactive damp and mould identification: staff must report all issues, void properties inspected before letting, tenancy audits check for hazards, and reports never dismissed as tenant lifestyle factors. Extensive procedures (sections 26–28) suggest this area either represents a historical gap in service or new Awaab's Law compliance costs.
findings.matters: Shift to proactive detection and treatment increases operational costs. The scale of new procedures and 'zero-tolerance' language suggest a resource-intensive service area, potentially reflecting remediation of previous backlogs or compliance gaps.
findings.figures: Damp and mould investigations within 10 working days (or 24 hours if acute risk); safety works within 5 working days of inspection; remedial works to commence within 12 weeks maximum
findings.quote: We adopt a zero-tolerance approach to damp and mould, shifting from reactive to proactive practices. Reports of damp and mould will never be dismissed or attributed to 'lifestyle' factors.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Housing Repairs and Maintenance Policy 2025
findings.headline: Awaab's Law creates new mandatory obligation to provide alternative accommodation if emergency repairs cannot be completed within 24 hours
findings.detail: New housing safety regulations require emergency hazards to be made safe within 24 hours. If safety works cannot be completed in this timeframe, the council must provide suitable alternative accommodation to the tenant until the hazard is resolved. This is a new legal liability creating a contingent cost for emergency repair delays.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand new legal liabilities affecting the housing revenue account. Alternative accommodation costs could be material if repair backlogs prevent the council meeting the 24-hour deadline. This represents a new mandatory cost driver not previously required.
findings.figures: 24 hours to investigate and make safe emergency hazards; 10 working days for significant hazards; 5 working days to commence safety works; 12 weeks maximum to start remedial works
findings.quote: If safety works cannot be completed within the statutory timeframe (24 hours for emergency hazards), the Council will offer suitable alternative accommodation until the hazard is resolved.

findings.paper_title: Health Scrutiny Committee Review 2024-25 Adult Social Care Accom
findings.headline: Housing department unable to build new adult social care accommodation due to competing priorities and cost constraints
findings.detail: The council's housing department will most likely not build new extra care accommodation for older adults because priorities are directed toward homelessness and overcrowded family housing. Barriers include inflation, building material costs, land scarcity (Islington has the second-highest population density in London), and competing demands on capital.
findings.matters: Inability to develop housing supply means the council remains structurally dependent on expensive spot purchasing and out-of-borough placements; reduces long-term cost control options and leaves demand pressures unmanaged
findings.figures: No new extra care units in pipeline; second-highest population density in London; limited land availability
findings.quote: the Council's Housing department would most likely not be able to build more extra care accommodation for the elderly as the priorities were greater in other areas including homelessness and families living in overcrowded accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Health Scrutiny Committee Review 2024-25 Adult Social Care Accom
findings.headline: Families in emergency temporary accommodation increased 29% year-on-year due to lack of alternative housing
findings.detail: The number of homeless families living in emergency accommodation (B&Bs, hostels) rose 29% in one year. This increase is driven by high private rental costs and insufficient affordable housing alternatives, directly compounding the temporary accommodation cost crisis.
findings.matters: Rising homelessness demand directly escalates the £2.25m overspend and indicates uncontrolled cost escalation risk unless supply-side solutions are found
findings.figures: 29% year-on-year increase in homeless families in emergency accommodation
findings.quote: the number of homeless families living in emergency accommodation such as B&Bs and hostels had increased by 29% in a year. This was due to lack of alternative accommodation available.

findings.paper_title: Health Scrutiny Committee Review 2024-25 Adult Social Care Accom
findings.headline: Adult social care forced to use costly spot purchasing instead of cheaper block contracts to meet accommodation demand
findings.detail: Adult Social Care cannot meet demand for accommodation through cost-effective block contracts and is increasingly purchasing individual placements on a spot basis. Spot-purchased accommodation costs over £750 per week more than block rates for supported living and extra care. Most out-of-borough placements are spot-purchased, driving up costs above negotiated block rates.
findings.matters: The council is unable to control costs through volume-negotiated contracts and is forced into more expensive ad-hoc purchasing, creating structural cost pressure and limiting value-for-money
findings.figures: Average difference over £750 per week between spot and block rates for supported living and extra care; £35m on physical support, £23m on learning disabilities, £12.6m on mental health accommodation (2024/25)
findings.quote: On average, the weekly cost of spot purchased accommodation was higher than the block rates for all accommodation types. The greatest difference was for Supported Living and Extra Care where the average difference was over £750.

findings.paper_title: Health Scrutiny Committee Review 2024-25 Adult Social Care Accom
findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation overspend of £2.25m in the current financial year
findings.detail: Islington is experiencing a significant overspend on temporary accommodation for homeless households. This is part of a wider London issue—the average overspend across London councils is £20 million. The overspend is driven by high private rental costs (11% of applicants are in full-time employment but cannot afford local rents) and lack of alternative accommodation.
findings.matters: A £2.25m overspend represents material budget pressure that reduces available resources for other council services and may require reserve drawdown or compensating savings elsewhere
findings.figures: £2.25 million overspend for 2024/25; £20 million average overspend across London councils; 11% of homeless applicants in full-time employment
findings.quote: Islington Council had an overspend of £2.25 million for temporary accommodation in the current financial year. It was advised that this was an ongoing issue across most London Councils with an average overspend of £20 million in London.

findings.paper_title: Procurement strategy report for pan-London sexual health e-services
findings.headline: The entire funding strategy depends on cost offsets from sexual health clinics that Finance has explicitly stated it cannot verify as achievable
findings.detail: Finance acknowledge that the council can only afford the e-service if in-person clinic testing shifts online, generating offsetting savings of £1.841m per year. However, they state this offset is unverified. If clinic services do not achieve these savings, even with optional modules removed, Islington faces a £0.141m+ annual budget pressure it cannot absorb.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs to know whether the council has contingency plans if the assumed clinic savings do not materialise, and what reserves are available to cover a structural shortfall
findings.figures: Required annual clinic cost offset: £1.841m; unverified by Finance
findings.quote: It is not possible for Finance to verify if this offset is realistic, but if costs run high, or activity levels are not sufficiently offset by cost reductions in clinic services then the optional modules will be discontinued. If it is not possible to achieve a net reduction in costs, the additional financial pressure will need to be met by reserves and or budget growth from the Public Health ringfenced grant.

findings.paper_title: Procurement strategy report for pan-London sexual health e-services
findings.headline: Nine-year contract contains no inflation protection, requiring the provider to absorb all cost escalation
findings.detail: The council's financial commitment is fixed for nine years with no inflation or cost escalation clause. The provider is contractually required to control and absorb costs throughout the term. For a contract of this value over this duration, this is an unusually stringent cost constraint.
findings.matters: The council's cost exposure is fixed but the provider faces unprotected cost pressure; if the provider cannot sustain delivery under cost inflation, service continuity or quality could be at risk
findings.figures: 9-year contract term; no inflation provision
findings.quote: This contract has no provision for inflation. Providers are expected to control costs throughout the length of the contract.

findings.paper_title: Procurement strategy report for pan-London sexual health e-services
findings.headline: Cost forecasts from City of London assume significant activity growth that does not match Islington's own historical experience
findings.detail: The City of London's estimate of £1.174m per year is based on growth assumptions, but Islington's own data shows activity levels 'have remained relatively stable over time'. Finance acknowledge this divergence but have used the higher figure 'for prudence'. If Islington's historical stability continues, actual costs could be materially lower than forecast, indicating the cost model may be conservative or misaligned.
findings.matters: Cost projections drive the funding requirement; material divergence between the forecast and historical data suggests uncertainty about actual commitment required
findings.figures: City of London forecast: £1.174m per year; Islington's own estimate based on stable activity: £0.987m per year
findings.quote: Cost estimates provided by the City of London have been used in this report for prudence, but if activity levels do remain stable, contract costs will be lower and will reduce any potential financial risk. It is expected based on Islington's own estimates of service use that the offset required would be much lower. It is expected based on Islington's own estimates of service use costs to be £0.987m per year

findings.paper_title: Procurement strategy report for pan-London sexual health e-services
findings.headline: Current budget of £0.8m per year does not cover the estimated service cost of £1.174m per year, creating a material funding gap
findings.detail: The procurement commits Islington to costs estimated at £1.174m annually based on City of London forecasts, but the current budget is only £0.8m. Finance explicitly cannot verify whether offsetting savings from clinic services will materialise. The annual funding gap of £0.374m would need to be covered from reserves or Public Health grant growth.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director must understand whether the council can sustain a £0.374m annual cost pressure, and what the fallback position is if clinic offsets fail to occur
findings.figures: Current budget £0.8m per year; estimated cost £1.174m per year; annual funding gap £0.374m
findings.quote: It is not possible for Finance to verify if this offset is realistic, but if costs run high, or activity levels are not sufficiently offset by cost reductions in clinic services then the optional modules will be discontinued. If the optional modules are removed the cost pressure reduces to £0.941m per year or £0.141 more than budget.

findings.paper_title: App.1. Q1 2025_26 corporate progress & performance update
findings.headline: Flats Above Shops food waste service rollout at risk of missing April 2026 statutory deadline
findings.detail: The council faces "a risk around the procurement timetable" for mandatory food waste collection. The service must be in place by April 2026 (statutory requirement), but procurement is currently in survey and documentation preparation phase.
findings.matters: Failure to meet statutory deadlines creates legal and reputational risk and may trigger audit findings or government intervention. Regulatory non-compliance is a financial risk factor.
findings.figures: Statutory deadline: April 2026; Current status: surveying properties and preparing procurement documentation
findings.quote: There is a risk around the procurement timetable to get this rolled out by April 2026 when the council is statutorily required to provide the service.

findings.paper_title: App.1. Q1 2025_26 corporate progress & performance update
findings.headline: Care leavers in education, employment or training declined to 58.7%, down from 61%
findings.detail: Performance on a key statutory metric (CYPYP20) deteriorated year-on-year. The council attributes this to cohort complexity and data recording issues but acknowledges the decline despite intensified support programmes.
findings.matters: A decline in care leaver outcomes despite additional investment ("YES programme", "House Project") suggests either unmet needs, cost insufficiency, or effectiveness challenges in delivering outcomes.
findings.figures: 58.7% of 19–21-year-old care leavers in EET in 2024-25, down from 61% in 2023-24
findings.quote: Provisional data suggest the percentage of 19–21-year-old care leavers in education, employment and training was 58.7% in 2024-25, down from 61% in previous year.

findings.paper_title: App.1. Q1 2025_26 corporate progress & performance update
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation placements surged 30.9% year-on-year, now 1,622 households
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation demand rose from 1,234 to 1,622 households in one year. Although Islington remains below London average (20 per 1,000 vs 16.4), the rate of growth signals mounting homelessness pressure and associated revenue spend on temporary housing.
findings.matters: Rapidly rising homelessness demand creates unfunded revenue commitments and signals acute housing shortage and social distress in the borough, a leading indicator of wider fiscal stress.
findings.figures: 1,622 households in temporary accommodation (31 March 2025), up 30.9% from 1,234 (31 March 2024); 1,014 with children, up 32.8% YoY
findings.quote: In Islington, 1,622 households were in temporary accommodation, a 30.9% increase from 31 March 2024.

findings.paper_title: App.1. Q1 2025_26 corporate progress & performance update
findings.headline: Building Safety Act compliance causing lift installation delays and tall building works slowdown
findings.detail: New regulatory requirements under the Building Safety Act 2022 have created delays in critical infrastructure works on tall buildings. The council has submitted 13 Building Safety Regulator applications and notes it is "actively working to improve our understanding and compliance".
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance delays increase project costs, extend capital delivery timescales, and signal potential gaps in council readiness for new statutory obligations.
findings.figures: 13 Building Safety Regulator applications submitted; process causing delays to lift installations and tall building works
findings.quote: This process has caused some delays in lift installations and tall building works, but we are actively working to improve our understanding and compliance with the new regulations.

findings.paper_title: App.1. Q1 2025_26 corporate progress & performance update
findings.headline: Wave 3 Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund stalled pending legal clarification on leaseholder liability
findings.detail: Major government-funded housing decarbonisation works (Wave 3) are on hold indefinitely pending confirmation of how "Florries Law" (restricting leaseholder contributions) applies. Wave 2 is complete but Wave 3's restart date is uncertain.
findings.matters: A council dependent on government capital funding faces revenue risk if matching funding or cost recovery mechanisms change, and uncertainty on major programmes affects cashflow and forward planning.
findings.figures: Wave 3 funding on hold; Wave 2 completed and received in full
findings.quote: However, the Wave 3 SHDF is currently on hold pending confirmation on Florries Law, which restricts leaseholder contributions.

findings.paper_title: App.1. Q1 2025_26 corporate progress & performance update
findings.headline: Finsbury Leisure Centre scheme cancelled, costing 100 council homes from delivery target
findings.detail: A planned capital scheme delivering 100 new council homes has been abandoned. The council notes this directly undermines their target to secure planning permission for 178 new homes and acknowledges the target "will be a challenge" as a result.
findings.matters: A cancelled scheme of this scale signals either budget constraint or delivery risk on the council's capital programme, and directly impacts housing supply commitments.
findings.figures: 100 homes lost from scheme; 178-home planning permission target now at risk
findings.quote: The target to secure planning permission for 178 council homes will be a challenge given the decision not to proceed with Finsbury Leisure Centre scheme which accounted for 100 new homes.

findings.paper_title: App.1. Q1 2025_26 corporate progress & performance update
findings.headline: Housing investment funding gap of £43m per year against available resources of £60m
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies an annual £43m funding shortfall for its 30-year housing investment plan. This gap directly drives the rise in homes falling below Decent Homes Standard, with 4% now non-compliant (up from 3.3%), as newly arising need for investment outstrips delivery capacity.
findings.matters: A council unable to fund essential housing maintenance and safety work signals structural capital constraints and deteriorating asset quality, directly affecting the council's balance sheet and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £43m annual funding gap (pre-spending review 2025); £60m annual investment resources available; 4% of homes non-decent (3.3% previous year)
findings.quote: Our investment funding gap of £43m per year (pre-spending review 2025), compared to our investment resources of £60m per year, illustrates the strain the council is under in delivering adequate investment to council homes.

findings.paper_title: Cover note EXEC Q1 2025-26 Delivery Plan progress performance update
findings.headline: Resident complaints and experience performance flagged as ongoing challenge; integrity of monitoring methods under review
findings.detail: The council identifies resident experience and complaints as a continuing challenge area. New management is conducting a review with specific focus on improving the integrity of monitoring and reporting methods, with refreshed KPIs proposed for Q2.
findings.matters: Acknowledged weaknesses in complaints and experience tracking, combined with need to improve monitoring integrity, suggest control gaps in operational management and service quality oversight.
findings.figures: No baseline performance cited; described as area requiring management review and KPI refresh
findings.quote: Performance for resident experience and complaints continue to be a challenge. These areas are undergoing a review by the new management including improvements to the integrity of monitoring and reporting methods.

findings.paper_title: Cover note EXEC Q1 2025-26 Delivery Plan progress performance update
findings.headline: Liveable Neighbourhoods programme delays: 37% of schemes in development but delayed for refinement
findings.detail: Coverage remains at 24% of the borough with permanent LTNs. A further 37% is in development but is experiencing delays as schemes are paused for additional refinement following engagement feedback.
findings.matters: Delays to major council infrastructure programmes, even when attributed to engagement rather than budget, indicate slower execution pace and may reflect resource or management constraints affecting service delivery.
findings.figures: 24% permanent LTN coverage; 37% in development (delayed)
findings.quote: As of Q1, Liveable Neighbourhoods (LN) still cover 24% of the borough (permanent LTN's). A further 37% is in development, but some schemes are delayed to allow for further refinement following engagement.

findings.paper_title: Cover note EXEC Q1 2025-26 Delivery Plan progress performance update
findings.headline: Finsbury Leisure Centre scheme cancelled, removing 100 new homes from housing delivery
findings.detail: The council has decided not to proceed with a capital scheme planned to deliver 100 council homes. As a result, the target to secure planning permission for 178 new council homes is now flagged as a challenge going forward.
findings.matters: Cancellation of a major capital scheme either reflects budget constraints or strategic reprioritisation; either indicates tighter capital control than originally planned and signals delivery risk on other projects.
findings.figures: 100 homes from cancelled scheme; 178 planning permission target now a challenge
findings.quote: The target to secure planning permission for 178 council homes will be a challenge given the decision not to proceed with Finsbury Leisure Centre scheme which accounted for 100 new homes.

findings.paper_title: Cover note EXEC Q1 2025-26 Delivery Plan progress performance update
findings.headline: Decent Homes Standard deteriorating; council attributes decline to investment challenge
findings.detail: 4% of homes did not meet Decent Homes Standard at end of 2024/25, up from 3.3% the previous year. The council explicitly links this to an investment challenge affecting London councils broadly, signalling housing stock maintenance is being deferred.
findings.matters: Rising non-compliance indicates the council lacks capacity to maintain its housing stock to required standards, a direct signal of constrained capital budgets and potential service quality risk.
findings.figures: 4% of homes non-compliant (2024/25), up from 3.3% (2023/24)
findings.quote: At the end of 2024/25, 4% of homes did not meet Decent Homes Standard – a small increase on the previous year (3.3%), reflecting the investment challenge that Islington, like other London Councils, is facing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Housing General Fund REFCUS Q1
findings.headline: Two major pipeline schemes, Vorley Road (£21.375m total) and Bemerton Estate South (£26.611m total), show significant 2025/26 slippage with spend concentrated in 2026/27.
findings.detail: Vorley Road is budgeted at £8.459m for 25/26 but forecast to deliver only £2.850m, with £13.277m now expected in 26/27. Bemerton is budgeted at £6.555m for 25/26 but forecast only £2.100m, with £15.375m deferred to 26/27. Both schemes are showing variances of over £4m in the current year.
findings.matters: Lenders assess multi-year capital commitments and delivery risk; deferring £13m and £15m respectively of large housing schemes into the next year concentrates delivery risk and may affect borrowing or grant drawdown timing.
findings.figures: Vorley Road: £8.459m budgeted 25/26, £2.850m forecast, £13.277m planned 26/27. Bemerton: £6.555m budgeted 25/26, £2.100m forecast, £15.375m planned 26/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Housing General Fund REFCUS Q1
findings.headline: The overall Housing General Fund capital programme is £23.2m behind forecast in Q1, with only £7.178m of £30.387m budgeted spend forecast for the year.
findings.detail: The programme was budgeted at £30.387m for 2025/26 but Q1 actuals and forecast total only £7.178m, a shortfall of £23.209m. This represents 76% of the year's expected spend now slipped.
findings.matters: Major slippage on a council's capital programme constrains cash flow, delays housing delivery, and may indicate systemic delivery challenges or re-profiling of the investment plan.
findings.figures: Total budget £30.387m, total forecast outturn £7.178m, total variance (£23.209m)
findings.quote: Housing General Fund Total | 30.387 | (0.405) | 7.178 | (23.209)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Housing General Fund REFCUS Q1
findings.headline: Finsbury Leisure Centre £10.649m pipeline scheme has zero Q1 delivery and has been fully removed from this year's forecast.
findings.detail: The scheme was budgeted at £10.649m for 2025/26 but the Q1 forecast outturn is zero. The paper requests a reduction of £10.649m, meaning the entire year's spend has slipped. This is a material capital scheme with no progress.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if the council can deliver major housing capital schemes; complete year slippage on a £10.6m project signals either delivery challenges or planning issues.
findings.figures: Budget £10.649m, Q1 forecast outturn £0m, requested reduction £10.649m
findings.quote: Finsbury Leisure Centre - Pipeline New Build | 10.649 | 0.005 | - | (10.649) | - | - | - | (10.649)

findings.headline: Proportion of council homes failing Decent Homes Standard has increased despite acknowledged investment gap
findings.detail: The share of council homes not meeting Decent Homes Standard has risen to 4% from 3.3% year-on-year. The council explicitly attributes this to inadequate investment levels facing Islington and other London councils, indicating capital underfunding is outpacing the pace of remedial work.
findings.matters: Rising non-compliance indicates insufficient capital investment in existing housing stock and signals either future borrowing needs or potential reserve drawdown to fund catch-up maintenance. Asset deterioration also risks tenant dissatisfaction and reputational damage.
findings.figures: 4% non-compliant (up from 3.3%)
findings.quote: At the end of 2024/25, 4% of homes did not meet Decent Homes Standard – a small increase on the previous year (3.3%), reflecting the challenge that Islington, like other London Councils, are facing due to inadequate investment.

findings.headline: Finsbury Leisure Centre scheme cancelled, removing 100 council homes from capital delivery plan
findings.detail: The council has decided not to proceed with the Finsbury Leisure Centre scheme, which was expected to deliver 100 of the 178 council homes required to meet the Delivery Plan's planning permission target for Q4 2025/26. This represents a 56% reduction in the target and will require other schemes to make up the shortfall to avoid missing the strategic objective.
findings.matters: A major capital project cancellation signals either financial constraint or planning/operational difficulty, and directly reduces the council's housing delivery track record. This affects borrowing assumptions and the credibility of future capital plans.
findings.figures: 100 homes cancelled from a 178 home target
findings.quote: The target to secure planning permission for 178 council homes will be a challenge given the decision not to proceed with Finsbury Leisure Centre scheme which accounted for 100 new homes.

findings.headline: Overspend mitigation depends on property acquisitions and reserve depletion
findings.detail: The reported £6.516m overspend is achieved only by offsetting £5.948m of additional income 'primarily driven by additional rental income for additional properties that have been purchased.' Additionally, reserves are being drawn to cover allegedly 'one-off' complaints and damp/mould costs. Without sustained property acquisitions, the true underlying overspend would approach £12.5m.
findings.matters: The apparent overspend mitigation rests on asset-dependent income and reserve drawdown; if acquisitions slow or capital spending moderates, the HRA would face a materially larger structural deficit.
findings.figures: £5.948m additional income; reliance on property acquisitions
findings.quote: There is currently additional income forecasted of -£5.948m. This is primarily driven by additional rental income for additional properties that have been purchased and leaseholder recharges linked to the acceleration of the Major works capital programme.

findings.headline: Pay award offer 3.2% exceeds 2.5% budget assumption; £0.6m risk
findings.detail: The 2025-26 pay award is not yet agreed. The current offer of 3.2% 'is above the budgeted assumption of 2.5%, resulting is a potential further pressure of around £0.6m to the HRA.' This is an uncontrolled cost pressure that could crystallize during the year.
findings.matters: An additional £0.6m pressure from pay awards would push the year-end overspend higher; this is not yet budgeted and represents downside risk to the current forecast.
findings.figures: 3.2% offer vs. 2.5% budget; £0.6m potential pressure
findings.quote: The 2025/26 pay award is yet to be agreed, the offer of 3.2% increase is above the budgeted assumption of 2.5%, resulting is a potential further pressure of around £0.6m to the HRA.

findings.headline: Management service restructure savings not yet delivered; recruitment ongoing
findings.detail: The HRA agreed £0.993m in savings for 2025-26, but 'Most savings are on track to be delivered this financial year except for the management service restructure saving which will not be fully delivered this year.' The restructure has completed but 'recruitment to posts is still underway.'
findings.matters: Savings slippage undermines the budget plan; delayed restructure savings create a gap in offsetting operational pressures when the account is already significantly in overspend.
findings.figures: £0.993m agreed savings; restructure savings not yet delivered
findings.quote: The HRA had agreed savings of £0.993m for 2025/26. Most savings are on track to be delivered this financial year except for the management service restructure saving which will not be fully delivered this year.

findings.headline: Repairs and maintenance overspend £1.379m creates feedback loop to claims
findings.detail: Repairs and maintenance are forecasting an overspend of £1.379m driven by 'increased volumes of jobs and inflationary pressures on contractor costs.' The paper explicitly flags the feedback mechanism: 'Failure to complete repairs can lead to increased complaints and potential disrepair cases which can cause further financial pressure on the HRA.'
findings.matters: Under-resourced repairs drive higher disrepair claims and complaints, multiplying costs; this feedback loop poses a risk that the current overspend could expand if repair workload grows faster than adjustments.
findings.figures: £1.379m overspend; increased volumes and inflationary pressure
findings.quote: Repairs and maintenance are currently forecasting an overspend of +£1.379m mainly due to increased volumes of jobs and inflationary pressures on contractor costs in recent years.

findings.headline: Damp and mould pressure £2.436m; budget still to be established
findings.detail: Damp and mould represents a forecast pressure of £2.436m (reducing to £1.415m after proposed budget adjustment). Notably, 'As part of the 2026-27 budget setting process work will be completed to establish a budget for damp and mould works'—indicating no formal budget currently exists for this category.
findings.matters: Damp and mould in social housing is a legal and regulatory risk (Building Safety Act, decent homes standards); the absence of an established budget suggests the council is still discovering the true cost and this pressure will resurface.
findings.figures: £2.436m pressure, reduced to £1.415m; budget to be established 2026-27
findings.quote: There is currently an expected pressure of +£2.436m in relation to damp and mould. A budget adjustment is proposed to help fund additional resources in relation to this which would reduce the pressure to +£1.415m. As part of the 2026-27 budget setting process work will be completed to establish a budget for damp and mould works.

findings.headline: Complaints overspend £1.247m amid 474% sector-wide increase
findings.detail: HRA complaints are forecast to overspend by £1.247m (reducing to £1.018m after proposed budget adjustment). This occurs against a backdrop of a 474% increase in complaints across the social housing sector from 2019-20 to 2024-25. Additional staffing resources are to be funded from HRA reserves 'given its one-off nature,' but the council notes this 'will need to be reviewed in the coming 12 months.'
findings.matters: Persistent and rising complaints suggest service quality or governance weaknesses; using reserves to cover allegedly 'one-off' costs indicates the baseline budget is structurally inadequate.
findings.figures: £1.247m overspend; 474% sector increase 2019-20 to 2024-25
findings.quote: There is a forecasted overspend of +£1.247m. A budget adjustment is proposed to help fund additional resources in relation to this which would reduce the overspend to +£1.018m. This budget adjustment will initially be covered from HRA reserves, given its one-off nature. This will, however, need to be reviewed in the coming 12 months.

findings.headline: Housing disrepair claims overspend £3.031m with elevated case volumes
findings.detail: Disrepair claims are forecasting an overspend of £3.031m, driven by 'elevated levels of disrepair cases, which are currently showing similar numbers as this time last year.' The council has agreed additional resources to reduce average awards per case and improve casework processing, but case volumes remain persistent.
findings.matters: Disrepair claims represent a contingent liability; persistent and elevated case volumes signal underlying property condition issues or procedural vulnerabilities that could worsen if repairs are further constrained.
findings.figures: £3.031m overspend; case volumes similar to prior year
findings.quote: There is a forecasted overspend of +£3.031m in relation to housing disrepair claims. This is mainly due to elevated levels of disrepair cases, which are currently showing similar numbers as this time last year.

findings.headline: HRA forecasting £6.516m net overspend for 2025-26
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is forecast to overspend by £6.516m. While this is partially offset by additional income of £5.948m (primarily from property acquisitions and leaseholder charges), the underlying operational pressures are substantial, covering disrepair claims, complaints, damp/mould, repairs, new build feasibility works, and temporary accommodation costs.
findings.matters: An overspend of this magnitude reflects persistent operational stresses across the HRA; a lender would be concerned about the council's ability to balance the account without sustained reliance on asset sales or reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £6.516m forecast overspend; £5.948m additional income offset
findings.quote: The HRA is forecasting a net overspend of + £6.516m.

findings.headline: Total capital programme £64m below forecast with £99.7m of slippage requested across all directorates
findings.detail: Across the entire capital programme, the council is requesting slippage of £99.686m against a revised budget of £316.223m. The overall forecast outturn is £252.198m, a variance of -£64.025m. Slippage is systemic across General Fund (£22.680m), HRA (£77.006m), and all service areas.
findings.matters: Large-scale systemic slippage indicates either financing delays, planning/regulatory bottlenecks, or reduced delivery capacity across the organisation. For a lender, this affects cash-flow forecasting, borrowing requirements, and covenant assumptions about capital delivery and asset investment.
findings.figures: Total budget £316.223m, forecast £252.198m, variance -£64.025m. Requested slippage -£99.686m (31.5% of revised budget).

findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grant demand-led overspend of £2.4m signals growth in adaptations for disabled residents
findings.detail: The DFG is budgeted at £0.724m but forecast at £3.131m, an overspend of +£2.407m (331% increase). Q1 actuals are £0.065m, showing this is forecast demand later in the year. This is a demand-led service where spend is driven by applications rather than budgeted capacity.
findings.matters: Uncontrollable demand-led overspends on disability services indicate either demographic change, policy commitment, or a backlog of applications. This signals a budget pressure point and tests the council's flexibility in managing social care commitments.
findings.figures: DFG budget £0.724m, actuals to 30.06.2025 £0.065m, forecast outturn £3.131m, variance +£2.407m.
findings.quote: Adult Social Care Disabled Facilities Grant 0.724 0.065 3.131 2.407

findings.headline: Finsbury Leisure Centre capital project substantially removed from 2025/26 delivery with combined slippage of £27.2m
findings.detail: Finsbury Leisure Centre spans both HRA (£21.525m budget) and General Fund (£8.707m budget). The HRA allocation is being removed entirely (virementing to zero forecast), while General Fund slips from £8.707m to £3.0m. Combined, the project totalled ~£30.2m budget but is now forecast at only ~£3m.
findings.matters: A major regeneration project being largely removed from annual delivery signals either project reprioritisation, financing withdrawal, or planning/delivery obstacles. For a lender, this flags changes to capital strategy or unforeseen barriers to project delivery.
findings.figures: HRA Finsbury Leisure Centre: budget £21.525m removed entirely. GF Finsbury: budget £8.707m, forecast £3.0m, variance -£5.707m. Combined variance -£27.232m.
findings.quote: HRA Finsbury Leisure Centre 21.525 - - (21.525); Environment Finsbury Leisure Centre Redevelopment 8.707 0.887 3.000 (5.707)

findings.headline: Bemerton Estate South, a flagship new-build housing scheme, has slipped £27.4m with nil spend in first quarter
findings.detail: Bemerton Estate South, budgeted at £29.538m, is forecast to deliver only £2.1m in 2025/26 with slippage of £27.438m. Actuals to 30 June 2025 are nil. This represents 93% of the annual budget being pushed back to future years in Q1.
findings.matters: Flagship new build schemes are key to demonstrating delivery capacity and meeting affordable housing targets. A 93% slip in Q1 suggests either planning delays, financing gaps, or delivery challenges. For lenders, this raises questions about the council's project management and its ability to execute on housing commitments.
findings.figures: Bemerton Estate South: budget £29.538m, actuals to 30.06.2025 £0m, forecast £2.1m, slippage £27.438m.
findings.quote: HRA Bemerton Estate South 29.538 - 2.100 (27.438)

findings.headline: HRA capital programme forecast £49.8m below budget with systemic slippage across major housing schemes
findings.detail: The HRA capital budget of £245.718m is forecast to deliver only £195.932m, a variance of -£49.786m. This reflects large slippages across multiple schemes: Bemerton Estate South (£27.438m), Vorley Road (£11.192m), Tall Blocks programme (£7.424m), and Harvist Estate (£8.281m). Requested acceleration of £48.745m is only partially offsetting requested slippage of -£77.006m.
findings.matters: The HRA represents the council's largest capital programme (78% of total). Systemic slippage across housing schemes indicates either planning/regulatory delays or financing constraints. For lenders, this affects both cash forecasting and the council's ability to deliver housing commitments, which are often tied to external funding and local strategy.
findings.figures: HRA budget £245.718m, forecast £195.932m, variance -£49.786m. Requested slippage -£77.006m. Bemerton Estate -£27.438m, Vorley Road -£11.192m, Harvist Estate -£8.281m, Tall Blocks -£7.424m.

findings.headline: Housing management service restructure saving of £0.130m marked as undeliverable
findings.detail: The planned restructure of Islington's housing management service was expected to deliver £130,000 in savings for 2025/26, but is now marked as undeliverable. This accounts for 13% of the council's £993,000 total HRA savings target. The council will need to secure alternative savings or absorb the cost within its HRA budget.
findings.matters: Lenders assessing the council's financial resilience need confidence that planned cost reductions will be delivered. An undeliverable saving indicates execution risk in the budget plan and signals potential pressure on HRA finances.
findings.figures: £0.130m undeliverable saving; total 2025/26 HRA savings target £0.993m
findings.quote: Housing management service restructure

findings.paper_title: Appendix_2B_2025-26_HRA Monitoring by Service Area Q1
findings.headline: Repairs and Maintenance is £4.074m over budget at Q1.
findings.detail: Repairs and Maintenance is forecast at £53.535m against a budget of £49.461m. This is the second-largest overspend and suggests maintenance demands exceed plan, either from deteriorating stock or reactive work displacing planned maintenance.
findings.matters: Repairs overspend can signal hidden stock quality problems, poor capital planning, or inflationary pressures in the market. It directly affects the council's ability to manage the housing stock and its capacity to invest in improvements.
