findings.quote: Repairs and Maintenance 49.461 53.535 4.074

findings.paper_title: Appendix_2B_2025-26_HRA Monitoring by Service Area Q1
findings.headline: General Management costs are running £9.902m over budget—a 13% overspend.
findings.detail: General Management is forecast at £85.677m against a budget of £75.775m. This single line accounts for the majority of the HRA's deficit and represents the most controllable expenditure area. The magnitude suggests either a severely underestimated budget or unplanned cost escalation.
findings.matters: General Management should be the most predictable cost in housing. A 13% overspend signals staffing inflation, unplanned operational pressures, or structural cost assumptions that have broken. Lenders need to know whether this is fixable in-year or structural.
findings.figures: Budget £75.775m; forecast £85.677m; overspend £9.902m
findings.quote: General Management 75.775 85.677 9.902

findings.paper_title: Appendix_2B_2025-26_HRA Monitoring by Service Area Q1
findings.headline: HRA has swung from a balanced budget to a £6.515m forecast deficit.
findings.detail: The budget was set to break even (0.000m surplus/deficit), but Q1 forecast shows a £6.515m deficit. Despite income outperforming budget by £5.680m across rents and charges, expenditure overruns of £12.196m are creating a significant hole that threatens HRA sustainability.
findings.matters: A £6.5m HRA deficit in the first quarter signals either a fundamentally flawed budget or cost pressures the council cannot control. This is material to repayment capacity and requires urgent remedial action.
findings.figures: Budget surplus 0.000m; forecast deficit 6.515m; total expenditure overspend 12.196m vs income outperformance 5.680m
findings.quote: (Surplus)/Deficit 0.000 6.515 6.516

findings.headline: Outsourcing of core in-house services including adult reablement and leisure provision
findings.detail: The council is procuring an external reablement service to replace current in-house delivery (£1.88m saving across 2027/28-2029/30) and moving leisure management to an agency model (£0.4m). Both represent shifts from direct council provision to external delivery.
findings.matters: Outsourcing creates dependency on external providers and reduces direct cost and quality control. Reablement in particular serves vulnerable adults and has safeguarding implications; service failure or provider collapse creates continuity risk
findings.figures: £1.880m (external reablement) + £0.400m (GLL agency model)
findings.quote: Procurement of an external reablement service, to deliver the current in-house service at a lower cost; Agency model for the GLL contract

findings.headline: Systematic cuts to Voluntary and Community Sector grants across multiple directorates, with one programme explicitly aiming for 30% reduction
findings.detail: The council is reviewing VCS contracts and grants across Children & Young People, Health & Social Care, Community Wealth Building, Environment and Homes & Neighbourhoods. One health and social care review explicitly aims to reduce grants to organisations by 30%. These cuts total over £1.2m across the five-year plan.
findings.matters: VCS grants typically fund early intervention and prevention services. Systematic defunding risks creating downstream demand pressure in social care and children's services, potentially increasing costs rather than reducing them
findings.figures: Health & Social Care 0.775m, across other directorates approximately £0.4m+
findings.quote: Review Voluntary Community Service grants programme review with aim to reduce number of grants to organisations by 30%

findings.headline: Headcount reduction of around 10% over three years accounts for £16.2m of the £29.4m savings programme
findings.detail: The council is planning to cut staffing by approximately 10% over three years, including a review of senior management. This represents 55% of the total planned savings and is the single largest savings measure.
findings.matters: At this scale, headcount reduction is a key risk factor for lenders: it affects service delivery capacity, can create demand risk if not matched to lower demand, and indicates the council is under significant budget pressure
findings.quote: Reduce the headcount of the organisation by around 10% over three years including a review of senior management and wider efficiencies

findings.headline: £1.021m emergency virement needed for HRA damp and mould remediation
findings.detail: The council has had to transfer £1.021m from HRA contingency specifically to address damp and mould issues, with a further £0.229m for HRA complaint handling. This was not in the original budget.
findings.matters: Damp and mould in social housing carries legal and reputational risk; the unbudgeted nature of this draw suggests the problem either emerged or escalated recently.
findings.figures: £1.021m Damp and Mould, £0.229m HRA complaints
findings.quote: HRA Virement for move budget £1.250m from HRA contingency, and increase the budget for Damp and Mould by £1.021m and increase the budget for HRA complaints by £0.229m

findings.headline: £5.400m headcount reduction target is only 53% on track, with £2.523m offset by other variances
findings.detail: A cross-cutting 10% headcount reduction over three years was planned to save £5.400m, but only £2.877m is on track while £2.523m is offset by other variances—suggesting recruitment has resumed or vacancies are being backfilled due to service pressures.
findings.matters: Failed workforce reductions indicate either service delivery needs have forced re-hiring or the council cannot sustain planned staff levels, suggesting underlying demand pressures.
findings.figures: Planned £5.400m, on track £2.877m, offset by variances £2.523m
findings.quote: Headcount Reduction: Reduce by 10% over three years, including senior management review. 0.000 5.400 5.400 2.877 2.523 0.000 0.000

findings.headline: £0.538m of enforcement and ASB service savings are undeliverable, suggesting operational capacity problems
findings.detail: Three enforcement initiatives—additional littering and environmental enforcement (£0.358m undeliverable), reconfigured out-of-hours ASB & Noise service (£0.130m undeliverable), and night-time waste crime enforcement (£0.050m undeliverable)—have all failed to deliver. Together these represent services the council cannot scale or restructure as planned.
findings.matters: Persistent failure to deliver enforcement savings suggests staffing constraints or operational difficulties that may affect council service delivery and income collection.
findings.figures: Additional enforcement £0.358m undeliverable, ASB/Noise service £0.130m undeliverable, night-time waste £0.050m undeliverable
findings.quote: Additional enforcement operations to increase the level of littering enforcement and other environmental enforcement. 0.358 ... 0.000 ... -0.358

findings.headline: Council now depends on £4.500m new income from increased parking charge notice rates to fund transport and environmental work
findings.detail: A single change to the PCN rate is estimated to generate £4.500m additional income, transferred from the parking account to general contingency to fund transport and environmental improvements. This represents material new income dependency on enforcement.
findings.matters: A significant portion of 2025/26 budget delivery depends on parking enforcement income; any reduction in enforcement activity or appeals success would create a shortfall.
findings.figures: £4.500m estimated PCN income increase
findings.quote: It is estimated the change in PCN rate will generate £4.500m for the council's parking account. This income will be used to fund transport and environmental improvements.

findings.headline: Council using £1.000m of contingency reserve to cover commercial property income shortfall
findings.detail: The Executive has approved using contingency to offset shortfalls in commercial property rents, with a strategy to dispose of or find alternative uses for properties that cannot be let. This indicates the council's commercial property portfolio is underperforming its budget.
findings.matters: Reliance on asset disposals to balance the budget is a last-resort position; a lender would want to understand the scale and timeline of planned property sales.
findings.figures: £1.000m virement from contingency
findings.quote: apply £1.000m of contingency budget to partially offset the shortfall in commercial property income. The Executive has approved a strategy to bring the remainder of the commercial income budget back into balance by disposing of or finding alternative uses for property that we cannot let.

findings.headline: £2.975m of planned 2025/26 savings are delayed or undeliverable, leaving only 58.8% on track
findings.detail: Of £17.632m total planned savings, only £10.372m are on track. A further £4.318m are offset by other variances (suggesting savings are happening but consumed by overspends elsewhere), while £0.688m are undeliverable and £2.287m are delayed. This represents material slippage in budget delivery.
findings.matters: If savings targets are not met, the council faces a widening budget deficit and may need to draw further on reserves or find additional income sources.
findings.figures: On track £10.372m, Undeliverable £0.688m, Delayed £2.287m, Offset by variances £4.318m

findings.headline: Staffing overspend of £0.888m signals structural cost pressure in HRA operations
findings.detail: General Management shows £0.888m staffing overspend in Q1. Unlike one-off compliance costs, staffing overruns typically represent permanent cost increases that recur through the year.
findings.matters: Staffing cost growth in HRA operations reduces headroom and constrains future service investment; it is a run-rate cost that cannot easily be reversed.
findings.figures: £0.888m (Q1); would annualize to ~£3.5m
findings.quote: General Management Overspend Staffing overspend 0.888

findings.headline: Total HRA overspend of £6.516m in Q1, driven by multiple service and compliance pressures
findings.detail: The HRA shows a combined overspend of £6.516m in the first quarter. This is before any assumptions about in-year savings or use of reserves. The overspends are concentrated in compliance and maintenance (disrepair, damp and mould, repairs totalling £6.847m) which are not discretionary.
findings.matters: An HRA overspend of this scale in Q1, annualizing to ~£26m, would be material to the council's overall position and may force reserve drawdown or require savings elsewhere to offset.
findings.figures: £6.516m total overspend; individual compliance/repairs costs total £6.847m
findings.quote: Total Housing Revenue Account 6.516

findings.headline: New build feasibility costs overrunning by £3.408m, raising questions about capital delivery timescale and cost control
findings.detail: General Management shows a £3.408m overspend on new build feasibility in Q1. This is the largest single variance and suggests the council's development pipeline is consuming more resource than planned, either through extended feasibility work or cost surprises emerging.
findings.matters: Oversized feasibility costs suggest either scope creep on pipeline projects or unexpected cost barriers; lenders need to know whether housing development assumptions are realistic.
findings.quote: General Management Overspend New build feasibility 3.408

findings.headline: Disrepair-related costs overrunning by £3.032m, indicating legal or regulatory pressure
findings.detail: General Management shows £3.032m overspend for disrepair-related costs in Q1. This suggests the council is either facing reactive legal costs or emergency remedial work beyond budget assumption. The scale indicates this is not a minor variance.
findings.matters: Disrepair cost overruns typically signal either unresolved maintenance backlogs or new legal claims; either way, they are structural pressures on the HRA that constrain future investment capacity.
findings.figures: £3.032m (Q1); would annualize to ~£12.1m
findings.quote: General Management Overspend Disrepair related cost 3.032

findings.headline: Damp and mould overspend of £2.436m in Q1, suggesting widespread housing stock compliance issues
findings.detail: Repairs and Maintenance shows a £2.436m overspend attributed to damp and mould in the first quarter alone. This is a major regulatory flashpoint following the Decent Homes crisis and suggests the council is dealing with significant stock condition problems. Annualized, this single issue would cost over £9.7m.
findings.matters: Damp and mould in social housing is a regulatory priority and reputational risk; persistent overspends signal either systemic stock problems or failure to estimate the true cost of compliance.
findings.figures: £2.436m (Q1); annualized ~£9.7m
findings.quote: Repairs and Maintenance Overspend Damp and Mould 2.436

findings.headline: Key FutureWork savings of £1.253m delayed until 2027-28 pending property leasing and redevelopment decisions
findings.detail: The council cannot deliver £1.253m of FutureWork savings in 2025-26 (£1.184m relate to prior year delays). These depend on leasing Laycock Street to the North Central Integrated Care Board or finding an alternative solution, and redevelopment of Newington Barrow Way for a GP surgery and temporary accommodation. Full delivery is not expected until 2027-28, representing a two-year delay.
findings.matters: Delayed savings indicate planned initiatives are not materialising as expected. This is a material amount of savings the council has committed to for multiple years and cannot deliver, signalling execution risk.
findings.figures: £1.253m total FutureWork savings delayed, £1.184m relate to prior year delays, delivery expected 2027-28
findings.quote: There is a delay to the delivery of £1.253m of FutureWork savings (£1,184m relate to prior years). Ongoing discussions about leasing Laycock Street to the North Central Integrated Care Board (ICB) or an alternative solution and the redevelopment of Newington Barrow Way (NBW) to provide a GP surgery and temporary accommodation will enable delivery of these savings in full by 2027/28.

findings.headline: Commercial property income shortfall of £1.133m due to weak rental market and further lease terminations
findings.detail: Commercial property income is forecasting a net shortfall of £1.133m due to shortfall in the rent roll and termination of a further lease at Old Street. The council has approved a strategy to dispose of or find alternative uses for property it cannot let, being implemented in 2025-26. The council applied £1.000m of corporate contingency to partially offset this.
findings.matters: Property disposals are a non-recurrent source of cash and cannot be relied upon indefinitely. The underlying rent roll weakness suggests asset quality or market issues that will persist.
findings.figures: £1.133m net income shortfall, £1.000m contingency applied, disposal strategy being implemented
findings.quote: There is a +£1.133m forecast net shortfall in income for commercial property due to an underlying shortfall in the rent roll and the termination of a further lease at Old Street. The Executive has approved a strategy to bring the remainder of the commercial income budget back into balance by disposing of or finding alternative uses for property that we cannot let.

findings.headline: Planning income shortfall of £1.110m reflects continued downturn in development activity, with 90% of budget reliant on fee income
findings.detail: Planning is forecasting a £1.110m income pressure due to shortfalls in planning fees, planning performance agreements, design review panel income and CIL income. Over 90% of the development management budget is reliant on income. The council notes the forecast "is subject to significant risk and variation throughout the year." Decline in development activity also creates wider funding risk for programmes dependent on CIL and S106 income.
findings.matters: A service where 90% of budget depends on discretionary income and facing a structural downturn is a significant sustainability risk. The council explicitly acknowledges high volatility and risk.
findings.figures: £1.110m planning income pressure, 90% of development management budget reliant on income
findings.quote: Planning are forecasting an income pressure of +£1.110m, mainly due to a continued downturn in planning activity affecting planning fees, planning performance agreements, design review panel income and CIL income. Over 90% of the development management budget is reliant on income, making it highly sensitive to reduced planning activity.

findings.headline: Local government pay offer of 3.2% vs 2.5% budgeted creates estimated recurrent pressure of £3.460m not yet funded
findings.detail: The local government pay offer for 2025-26 is 3.2% on NJC pay points and allowances. The council budgeted for 2.5%, creating an estimated pressure of £3.460m. Critically, the council describes this as "a recurrent pressure that would need to be factored into 2026/27 budget setting." At report date, the offer has not been accepted by unions, creating further uncertainty.
findings.matters: This is a structural cost pressure on the council's baseline that persists beyond 2025-26. If accepted, it requires either £3.460m of savings or other funding starting next year, with the outcome still uncertain.
findings.figures: 3.2% pay offer vs 2.5% budgeted, £3.460m estimated pressure, £6.340m total corporate pay award budget
findings.quote: A 3.2% offer would create an estimated pressure of £3.460m based on the latest calculation. This would be a recurrent pressure that would need to be factored into 2026/27 budget setting.

findings.headline: School balances projected to fall into net deficit after 2025-26, with 14 schools already in deficit
findings.detail: School balances were £5.293m at end of 2024-25 but are composed of 14 schools in deficit and 34 in surplus. Balances are projected to fall to £0.899m by end of 2025-26, "after which they will fall into a net deficit." Decline since 2019-20 reflects falling pupil rolls, increasing costs and funding not keeping pace with inflation.
findings.matters: Schools moving into a net deficit position signals emerging sustainability issues in the education sector that will require intervention. This interconnects with the DSG High Needs pressure and represents a second major education finance problem.
findings.figures: £5.293m balance end 2024-25, 14 schools in deficit, 34 in surplus, £0.899m projected end 2025-26, then net deficit thereafter
findings.quote: School balances have been in decline since 2019/20 due to falling pupil rolls, increasing costs and funding which has not kept pace with inflation. The balance at the end of 2024/25 was a net surplus of £5.293m however this is made up of 14 schools in deficit and 34 schools in surplus. Balances are projected to reduce to £0.899m net surplus by the end of 2025/26 after which they will fall into a net deficit.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation cost pressure is structural and will persist, with case numbers up 66% in one year and nightly rates rising 15%
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation is forecasting a £0.472m Q1 overspend, but underlying pressures are much larger. Case numbers rose 66% in 2024-25 against a budgeted assumption of 60% growth. Nightly rates rose over 15% in 2024-25. Additional pressures include £1.074m bad debt overspend (rent arrears) and £0.365m prevention spend. The council explicitly states: "it is likely that the financial pressure will remain for the medium term."
findings.matters: This is a structural cost pressure driven by the housing and cost-of-living crises. The council's own assessment is that cost pressures will not abate locally or nationally, making this a persistent drain on finances.
findings.figures: £0.472m Q1 overspend, 66% case number growth in 2024-25, 15% nightly rate growth, £1.074m bad debt overspend, £0.365m prevention spend overspend
findings.quote: Numbers in TA are rising. Budget setting assumptions assumed a 60% increase in case numbers following the rise anticipated nationally. London has been the epicentre of homeless crisis, and Islington is no exception with case numbers rising by over 66% in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block heading into deficit as EHCP demand grows 9% annually while funding grows only 3%
findings.detail: The DSG High Needs Block is forecasting a £2.751m in-year overspend. Islington's DSG reserve of £3.909m will be substantially depleted to £0.914m by end of 2025-26. The DfE requires a Deficit Management Plan for councils experiencing net deficits or substantial reserve reductions. London Councils reports the combined deficit of all London boroughs will total £500m by end of 2025-26, showing this is not a local anomaly.
findings.matters: Running down reserves to cover recurrent deficits is unsustainable. This council faces a structural funding gap in SEND that will require either service reduction or ongoing reserve drawdown, with no obvious solution in the medium term.
findings.figures: £2.751m HNB overspend, 9% annual EHCP growth vs 3% funding growth, £3.909m opening DSG reserve, £0.914m projected closing balance, £500m combined London DSG deficit forecast
findings.quote: The HNB funds educational provision and support for children and young people with EHCPs. The number of children and young people with EHCPs has been growing on average by 9% per year over the last few years and funding has grown by only 3% per year. London Councils recently published figures suggesting that the combined deficit of all London boroughs will total £500m by the end of 2025/26.

findings.headline: Council housing operations £2.5m over budget in first quarter
findings.detail: New Homes & Corporate Landlord is forecast at £9.894m against budget of £7.348m, with £2.546m already overspent in Q1.
findings.matters: Cost pressure on the council's own housing investment programme early in the year suggests either structural overruns or delivery issues affecting the return on housing capital

findings.detail: Temporary accommodation spend is forecast at £14.179m against budget of £12.515m, with £1.664m already overspent in the first quarter. Annualized, this trajectory would exceed budget by £6.6m.
findings.matters: Homelessness is demand-driven and difficult to control; this early pressure indicates the council faces sustained cost pressure on a statutory obligation

findings.paper_title: Appendix_1B_2025-26_GF Revenue Monitoring by Service Area Q1
findings.headline: Capital financing forecast deteriorated by £8.7m
findings.detail: The budget showed capital financing delivering a £3.0m surplus, but Q1 forecasts a £5.7m cost. This reversal suggests either accelerated borrowing needs or unplanned financing pressures have emerged.
findings.matters: A material swing in the financing position signals potential pressure on debt sustainability and may require additional borrowing
findings.figures: Budget £3.036m income, forecast (£5.693m) cost, variance (£8.728m)

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Capital Budget Monitoring Report, Quarter 1 2025-26 - Executive Dispatch
findings.headline: Construction inflation forecast at 14% over five years with National Insurance rises of 16%, threatening capital project viability
findings.detail: The paper cites BCIS prediction of 14% building cost increases over the next 5 years to 2030, combined with a 16% forecast increase in National Insurance Contributions and National Living Wage costs over the same period. The council notes this is causing project business cases to no longer hold, leaving it needing either to increase budgets (requiring additional borrowing) or reduce project scope. Interest rates currently at 4.25% add to the cost of capital.
findings.matters: Sustained construction cost inflation erodes the council's purchasing power from its capital budget and forces difficult choices between scope reduction and increased borrowing. Higher interest rates make additional borrowing more expensive.
findings.figures: UK inflation (CPI) 3.6% year to July 2025; BCIS forecast 14% building cost increase 2025-2030; National Insurance/Living Wage forecast 16% increase 2025-2030; Bank Rate 4.25%
findings.quote: Inflation and interest rates pose key risks to the capital programme by placing financial pressures on affordability.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Capital Budget Monitoring Report, Quarter 1 2025-26 - Executive Dispatch
findings.headline: Building Safety Regulation delays affecting tall blocks investment programme (£5.807m)
findings.detail: The Tall Blocks project is experiencing significant delays due to external Building Safety Regulation approvals. The paper explicitly states that spend is now likely to fall into future years. This is a regulatory constraint beyond the council's control but indicates dependencies on external approvals for large capital commitments.
findings.matters: External regulatory delays affect when capital is deployed and revenues are spent, potentially pushing costs into later years when interest rates and inflation may be higher. Housing investment delays affect the council's delivery against housing targets.
findings.figures: Tall Blocks project budget £5.807m; budget slippage of £7.424m from 2025/26
findings.quote: Because of the nature of the works, external Building Safety Regulation applications and approvals are required for which there are ongoing significant delays, which means that some of the spend is now likely to fall into future years.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Capital Budget Monitoring Report, Quarter 1 2025-26 - Executive Dispatch
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £99.686m (32% of 2025/26 budget) indicates significant delivery delays across portfolio
findings.detail: At Q1, requested slippage from 2025/26 totals £99.686m, split £22.680m General Fund and £77.006m HRA. Reasons cited are broadly 'alignment to revised delivery plan' or project-specific issues like contractor failure. This represents near a third of the annual capital budget moving into future years, suggesting either over-ambitious planning or systematic delivery challenges.
findings.matters: Large-scale slippage indicates the council cannot deliver its planned capital investment on schedule. This affects the council's service delivery commitments, housing supply, and the revenue costs of borrowing spread over longer periods.
findings.figures: Slippage £99.686m (32% of 2025/26 budget at 2024/25 outturn of £316.223m); acceleration £50.713m (16%) partially offsets this
findings.quote: At Q1, the request slippage from 2025/26 is £99.686m, split between £22.680m General Fund and £77.006m HRA. This is equivalent to 32% of the 2025/26 capital budget as at 2024/25 outturn.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Capital Budget Monitoring Report, Quarter 1 2025-26 - Executive Dispatch
findings.headline: Two separate contractor administrations have delayed capital projects and forced re-procurement
findings.detail: The Decarbonisation Schemes project (Richard Cloudesley School) was delayed when the initial contractor entered administration, forcing a new procurement exercise. The Andover Estate current new build (42 units) was similarly delayed when the previous contractor went into administration, with the scheme completion now expected to slip. These are concrete examples of delivery risks materializing.
findings.matters: Contractor failures increase delivery timescales, costs, and procurement complexity. They indicate market stress in the construction sector and reduce the pool of viable suppliers.
findings.figures: Decarbonisation scheme budget slippage £1.020m; Andover Estate affected but completion still expected 2025/26
findings.quote: Following the falling into administration of the previous contractor there was a delay in procuring a new contractor to complete the scheme.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Capital Budget Monitoring Report, Quarter 1 2025-26 - Executive Dispatch
findings.headline: Finsbury Leisure Centre redevelopment cancelled after Executive decision in April 2025, removing £56.422m from 10-year capital programme
findings.detail: The council approved cessation of the redevelopment project and withdrew the planning application. The paper states that costs incurred to date on the housing elements will be written off to revenue within the HRA. The council plans to seek delivery of affordable housing elsewhere and make separate investment in the leisure centre and sports pitches. This represents a significant capital write-off and delivery failure.
findings.matters: A major capital scheme failure indicates either poor initial planning, changing circumstances, or delivery capability issues. Write-offs directly impact reserves and borrowing ratios.
findings.figures: £56.422m reduction across 10-year programme; costs incurred to date written off to HRA revenue
findings.quote: At the meeting of the Executive on Thursday 24th April 2025 the cessation of the current project to redevelop the Finsbury Leisure Centre site and the withdrawal of the associated planning application was approved.

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Capital Budget Monitoring Report, Quarter 1 2025-26 - Executive Dispatch
findings.headline: Capital programme forecast overspend of £0.129m despite budget controls
findings.detail: The General Fund capital budget is forecast to overspend by £0.129m against the £254.340m total capital programme. The report states that mitigating actions are being explored but does not detail what these are or their likelihood of success. This is small in percentage terms but indicates active budget pressure.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the council can control capital spending. An overspend, however small, on budget shows the council is not tracking delivery to plan.
findings.figures: Forecast overspend £0.129m; total 2025/26 capital programme £254.340m
findings.quote: This includes a forecast overspend of £0.129m to budget, for which mitigating actions are being explored.

findings.headline: Council is objecting to Fair Funding Review 2.0 formula as fundamentally flawed for urban high-cost areas
findings.detail: Islington has submitted detailed objections to the government's funding reform proposals, arguing they disproportionately disadvantage London boroughs and other high-cost urban areas. Key criticisms include: removal of urban weightings in highways funding; inadequate recognition of urban cost pressures; flawed council tax equalisation using a national average (£2,000) when Islington's actual Band D is significantly lower; reliance on outdated historical spending data that entrenches past underfunding; and removal of ethnicity indicators from children's formula. The council is in dialogue with government and other London boroughs about these issues.
findings.matters: If the government proceeds with the formula as proposed despite council objections, Islington would face material and unexpected funding reductions that cannot be planned for until December 2025
findings.figures: Notional national average council tax £2,000 (Islington's actual Band D significantly lower); formula changes phased over 2026–29
findings.quote: The use of a notional national average council tax level (£2,000) for equalisation is opposed by the council. Islington's actual Band D rate is significantly lower, and the formula offers no mechanism to adjust for this.

findings.headline: Council implementing spending restrictions and preparing to draw reserves if government funding cuts materialise
findings.detail: The council has placed spending controls in the current financial year including restrictions on agency use, recruitment, and vacancy management. For the medium term, the council is preparing to use one-off resources from reserves to bridge recurrent budget gaps 'in exceptional circumstances' if Fair Funding Review impacts are as modelled. General Fund reserves stand at 45% of Core Spending Power (£87m total), but budget-risk-only reserves are just 26% of CSP, indicating limited flexibility.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns to cover recurrent deficits are unsustainable; spending controls can reduce service quality and signal financial stress to the market
findings.figures: GF reserves 45% of CSP (end 2024/25); budget risk reserves 26% of CSP; total budget risk reserves £87m (£25m Budget Risk, £25m Core Funding Reserve, £37m GF Balance)
findings.quote: To prepare for the possible implications of Fair Funding Review 2.0 and maintain council reserves, spending controls have been put in place the current financial year. This involves continued restrictions on agency use, recruitment, and vacancy management, along with any other measures that may be considered necessary.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account under strain from £12m+ in concurrent pressures (damp, repairs, safety, disrepair claims)
findings.detail: The 2024/25 outturn reveals multiple concurrent pressures: £2.5m damp and mould, £4m repairs and maintenance, £2m building safety requirements, and £3.5m housing disrepair claims. Repairs cost inflation is significantly outpacing rental income growth due to government rent caps, narrowing the HRA's financial headroom. The council faces difficult trade-offs between maintaining existing stock and building new homes. Some mitigation from 10-year rent settlement (CPI +1%) and potential right-to-buy policy changes.
findings.matters: HRA deficits and overspends can spill into General Fund and erode available reserves; repair cost escalation against capped rental income reduces financial flexibility
findings.figures: 2024/25 pressures: ~£2.500m damp/mould, ~£4.000m repairs/maintenance, ~£2.000m building safety, £3.500m disrepair claims; potential additional £2m/year from rent convergence if government approves
findings.quote: The 2024/25 financial outturn saw the impact of continuing pressures. These were in line with the wider national housing sector and included ~£2.500m pressure on Damp and Mould, ~£4.000m on repairs and maintenance, ~£2.000m on Building Safety requirements, and £3.500m from Housing disrepair claims, which remain at elevated levels.

findings.headline: School balances forecast to move into net deficit in 2026/27 amid unfunded EHCP growth
findings.detail: School balances are expected to fall into net deficit in 2026/27 due to falling pupil numbers and above-inflation cost increases. The High Needs Block (funding for children with Education, Health and Care Plans) faces structural underfunding: the number of EHCPs has grown by approximately 9% per year but funding has grown by only 3% per year. London boroughs' combined DSG deficit is projected to total £500m by end 2025/26.
findings.matters: DSG deficits must eventually be resolved from General Fund or reserves; the 9% annual EHCP growth is a demand-side pressure that current funding mechanisms cannot sustain
findings.figures: EHCP numbers growing 9% per annum; funding growing 3% per annum; London boroughs combined DSG deficit projected £500m by end 2025/26
findings.quote: School balances are expected to continue to decline due to falling school numbers and above-inflation cost increases. It is anticipated that school balances will fall into a net deficit position in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Previously agreed savings of £18.7m flagged as at-risk and requiring replacement proposals
findings.detail: Savings totalling £6.914m in 2026/27 and £11.8m in 2027/28 (£18.714m total) were agreed in the 2025/26 budget but are now 'considered at risk of being undelivered, mainly where they need to be worked up into more specific proposals'. The council states it will develop and report these replacement proposals as part of the 2026/27 budget process. The MTFS depends on delivery of all previously agreed savings, so re-specification creates delivery risk.
findings.matters: If these savings do not materialise, the council faces an additional £18.7m budget gap requiring further service reductions or reserve drawdowns
findings.quote: Previously agreed savings that are considered at risk of being undelivered, mainly where they need to be worked up into more specific proposals, have been added back to the budget gap. Proposals to deliver these savings are currently being developed and will be reported to the Executive as part of the 2026/27 budget report process.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand and costs spiralling at 15-16% annual rate with no endpoint
findings.detail: Islington experienced a 66% increase in temporary accommodation demand in 2024/25. The MTFS forecasts a further 15.6% increase in 2026/27. Non-pay (rental) inflation is forecast at 15% for 2026/27, based on actual 2024/25 cost increases, then using industry predictions for later years. This is a statutory obligation that cannot be cut. The council describes it as an 'exponentially increasing problem' driven by the housing crisis, cost of living crisis, and legislative changes.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a non-discretionary cost growing faster than general inflation, consuming a rising share of revenue budget with limited levers to control it
findings.figures: 66% increase in demand in 2024/25; 15.6% assumed increase in 2026/27; contract inflation 15% in 2026/27 based on 2024/25 actuals; ONS rental growth 12.8% year-on-year (September 2024)
findings.quote: Homelessness and Temporary Accommodation is an exponentially increasing problem for local authorities all around the UK and Islington is no exception. There has been a 66% increase in demand in 2024/25 in Islington.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care demographic growth of £3.9m annually plus £9.6m management action investment, with ongoing delivery risk
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is the council's largest demographic pressure, growing from £3.916m in 2026/27 to £5.618m by 2029/30. The service has implemented a £9.578m management action programme over five years including systematic care package reviews, reablement initiatives, and integrated quality assurance processes. Growth is driven by ageing population, increased prevalence of learning disabilities, and NHS backlogs. Success depends on execution of these management actions.
findings.matters: If management actions fail to deliver, Adult Social Care overspends will erode reserves and force unpredictable additional spending cuts elsewhere
findings.quote: Adult Social Services continues to experience significant demographic pressures across all primary areas of support, including Memory and Cognition, Physical Support, Learning Disabilities, and Mental Health. These challenges are driven by increasing demand for services, greater requirements for acute care, and rising levels of need among existing service users.

findings.headline: Budget deficit could nearly double if Fair Funding Review proposals are implemented as currently drafted
findings.detail: The council faces a base budget gap of £15.617m in 2026/27 and £75.203m over five years. If the government's Fair Funding Review 2.0 proposals proceed as currently modelled, this would add an additional £14.6m in 2026/27 alone (total cumulative impact £45.090m over the period). The council is objecting to the proposals as flawed and damaging to London boroughs, but the actual impact will not be known until the December 2025 settlement announcement.
findings.matters: A potential doubling of the deficit would be material to the council's repayment capacity, likely requiring forced service reductions or unexpected reserve drawdowns
findings.figures: Net budget gap £15.617m (2026/27 before Fair Funding); £30.217m if Fair Funding goes ahead; cumulative decrease in funding £45.090m over MTFS period
findings.quote: The actual impact will not be known until the Provisional Local Government Finance settlement in late December 2025.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - Q1 Budget Monitoring and Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: Interest payable £7.483m below budget (forecast £3.000m v budget £10.483m), temporarily masking operational deficits
findings.detail: Corporate items are forecasting a £8.212m underspend, primarily from a £7.483m underspend on interest payable due to lower-than-budgeted borrowing and higher interest rates generating additional interest income. This one-off benefit masks the £9.752m underlying directorate overspend, allowing the reported General Fund overspend to remain only £1.540m.
findings.matters: A £7.483m interest underspend suggests the council budgeted more conservatively for borrowing than it required, or that interest rates have moved favourably. This is a one-off benefit masking structural operational problems. If borrowing needs grow or rates fall, this benefit disappears and the council's true position (£9.752m - £8.212m corporate benefit = £1.540m) becomes the baseline, with no headroom.
findings.figures: £7.483m interest payable underspend; forecast £3.000m v budget £10.483m
findings.quote: includes a -£7.483m underspend on interest payable, as the forecast for the year is £3.000m against a budget of £10.483m. The lower borrowing requirement and higher interest rates have also contributed to additional interest income.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - Q1 Budget Monitoring and Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: £0.688m in savings forecast to remain undelivered, plus £2.287m delayed to future years (17% of total MTFS savings at risk)
findings.detail: Of £17.632m in total savings to be delivered in 2025/26 (current year plus carried-forward), 83% (£10.372m) is on track or offsettable within services. However, 13% (£2.287m) is expected to be delayed to future years and 4% (£0.688m) is likely to remain undelivered. Undelivered savings include £0.588m in Homes & Neighbourhoods and £0.100m in Environment & Climate Change. Directorates are assessing whether delayed savings are genuinely delayed or unachievable.
findings.matters: Undelivered and delayed savings signal that planned efficiency gains are not materialising. This means the council is running a larger underlying deficit than the budget assumed and is now funding the gap with underspends elsewhere. If those underspends (e.g., interest payable benefit) reverse, the structural deficit emerges.
findings.figures: £17.632m total savings; £0.688m undeliverable (4%); £2.287m delayed (13%); £10.372m on track (83%)
findings.quote: Of this, 83% (£10.372m) is currently on track to be delivered in-year or expected to be offset by other variances within services (£4.318m). A further 13% (-£2.287m) is expected to be delayed to future years and 4% (£-0.688m) is likely to remain undelivered.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - Q1 Budget Monitoring and Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: SEND transport overspend of £0.617m from continued growth in young people requiring transport and rising unit costs
findings.detail: Special Educational Needs and Disabilities transport is forecasting a £0.617m overspend driven by continued growth in the numbers of young people requiring transport and rising costs to meet increased demand. Mitigations include Personal Transport Budgets, independent travel training, route optimisation, and contract reviews.
findings.matters: SEND transport demand is rising structurally while unit costs increase, creating a dual squeeze. This is a special needs population that cannot easily be substituted or deterred. Growth in SEND cohorts often signals rising prevalence of recognised need or improved identification; costs rising faster than volume suggests contract/provider cost inflation or service quality pressure.
findings.figures: £0.617m SEND Transport overspend
findings.quote: SEND Transport is forecasting a +£0.617m overspend due to the continued growth in the numbers of young people requiring transport and the rising costs to meet increased demand.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - Q1 Budget Monitoring and Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation bad debts forecast at £1.073m despite numbers rising more slowly than prior year
findings.detail: Bad debt and rent arrears in temporary accommodation are forecast to overspend by £1.073m. This sits alongside a direct cost overspend of £0.472m from rising nightly rents and increased average length of stay, despite new case numbers growing at a slower rate (27 per month versus 33 last year). Mitigations include property acquisition, allocations policy revision, prevention incentives, and improved rent collection.
findings.matters: A £1.073m bad debt position in temporary accommodation, even as case growth slows, indicates deteriorating tenant ability to pay (whether due to benefit delays, employment instability, or rent levels outpacing support). This is a welfare cliff signal and suggests the population in temporary housing is becoming more vulnerable, not less.
findings.figures: £1.073m bad debt and rent arrears overspend; £0.472m direct overspend; average 27 new cases per month (down from 33)
findings.quote: bad debt and rent arrears alone forecast to overspend by +£1.073m

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - Q1 Budget Monitoring and Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: Planning income down £1.110m from continued downturn in planning activity, flagged as a wider funding risk
findings.detail: Planning income is £1.110m below budget, reflecting continued decline in planning application volumes affecting fees, agreements, and Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) income. The council is adopting a prudent approach to forecasting and exploring fee structure reviews and service efficiency improvements.
findings.matters: A £1.110m planning income shortfall from persistent downturn in planning activity indicates economic weakness or reduced development activity in the borough. The paper explicitly flags this as a 'wider funding risk', suggesting planners expect it to persist. This is structural, not cyclical.
findings.figures: £1.110m planning income shortfall
findings.quote: a shortfall in planning income of +£1.110m, reflecting a continued downturn in planning activity affecting fees, agreements, and CIL income, which also poses a wider funding risk.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - Q1 Budget Monitoring and Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: Commercial property income shortfall of £1.133m due to reduced rent roll and lease terminations
findings.detail: Commercial property assets are forecasting a £1.133m income shortfall arising from a reduced rent roll and lease terminations. The Executive has approved a disposal and alternative-use strategy to bring the commercial income budget back into balance during 2025/26.
findings.matters: A £1.133m commercial property income loss indicates asset deterioration or market conditions preventing lettings. The council is now disposing of or finding alternative uses for properties it cannot let, which suggests sustained asset underperformance and potential further capital write-downs.
findings.figures: £1.133m commercial property income shortfall
findings.quote: Commercial Property Income is forecasting a +£1.133m shortfall in income due to a reduced rent roll and lease terminations as well as a shortfall in planning income of +£1.110m, reflecting a continued downturn in planning activity affecting fees, agreements, and CIL income, which also poses a wider funding risk.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - Q1 Budget Monitoring and Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: Parking income shortfall of £1.744m across multiple revenue streams
findings.detail: Parking services are forecasting a £1.744m overspend driven by income shortfalls across Pay & Display, suspension, permits, vouchers, and road closure income. Mitigation includes debt collection, fraud prevention, technology upgrades, and anticipated income from statutory increases in Penalty Charge Notice charges.
findings.matters: A £1.744m parking income shortfall indicates demand/usage decline rather than collection issues. This is a structural income vulnerability; the mitigations (technology, fraud prevention) address collection efficiency, not underlying demand. Statutory PCN charge increases are outside the council's direct control.
findings.figures: £1.744m parking overspend from income shortfalls
findings.quote: Parking is forecasting a +£1.744m overspend, mainly from income shortfalls across several streams including Pay & Display, suspension, permits and vouchers, and road closure income.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - Q1 Budget Monitoring and Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: HRA deficit of £6.516m driven by damp and mould remediation (£2.436m) and housing disrepair claims (£3.032m)
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account faces a ringfenced in-year deficit of £6.516m that will be funded from HRA reserves. The two largest pressure areas are £2.436m to tackle damp and mould in dwellings and £3.032m for elevated levels of housing disrepair claims requiring additional resources. These are policy and liability-driven issues, not demand or demand variables.
findings.matters: A £6.516m HRA reserve drawdown represents a significant one-year depletion of housing reserves and signals material building condition and liability issues. Damp and mould remediation is a regulatory and reputational risk; housing disrepair claims indicate possible failures in maintenance standards and legal exposure.
findings.figures: £6.516m in-year HRA deficit; £2.436m damp and mould pressure; £3.032m housing disrepair claims
findings.quote: The forecast position for the HRA is an in-year deficit of £6.516m. As the HRA is a ringfenced account, any deficit at the end of the financial year will be transferred from HRA reserves. The largest pressures within the HRA relate to a +£2.436m pressure arising from the need to tackle damp and mould in dwellings and +£3.032m pressure because of elevated levels of housing disrepair claims which require additional resources.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - Q1 Budget Monitoring and Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: General Fund overspend of £1.540m with underlying directorate pressures of £9.752m
findings.detail: Directorates are forecasting a combined overspend of £9.752m at Q1, primarily driven by Community Wealth Building (£3.776m), Environment & Climate Change (£4.223m), and Street Operational Services (£1.866m). This is partially offset by a £8.212m underspend in corporate items, mostly from lower capital expenditure and a £7.483m underspend on interest payable. The net position is a £1.540m overspend.
findings.matters: While the reported overspend is modest at Q1, the underlying operational pressures total £9.752m and are being masked by one-off corporate gains, primarily lower-than-budgeted interest costs. This suggests structural problems that may not persist if interest rates fall further.
findings.figures: £1.540m General Fund overspend; £9.752m directorate overspend; £8.212m corporate items underspend; £7.483m interest payable underspend (forecast £3.000m against budget £10.483m)
findings.quote: the General Fund (GF) revenue budget is forecast to overspend by +£9.752m at the directorate level, with the most significant pressure arising in Community Wealth Building, Environment and Climate Change and Housing GF directorates.

findings.paper_title: Appendix_1A_2025-26_GF Revenue Monitoring by Variance Q1
findings.headline: SEND Transport demand escalating at £0.617m overspend in Q1
findings.detail: Young people accessing home-to-school transport rising faster than budget. This is a demand-driven cost in a specialist service area with limited discretion.
findings.matters: Growing SEND transport costs are a structural service pressure; unlike discretionary spending, this cannot be easily contained if demand continues to rise.
findings.figures: £0.617m Q1 overspend
findings.quote: SEND Transport - Increase in young people accessing home to school transport

findings.paper_title: Appendix_1A_2025-26_GF Revenue Monitoring by Variance Q1
findings.headline: Commercial income and planning income shortfalls point to economic slowdown
findings.detail: New Homes and Corporate Landlord directorate reporting £1.133m forecast shortfall in commercial income alongside increased lease costs. Planning and Development showing £1.110m income shortfall due to downturn in development activity. These signals move together.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's commercial income base and development-related fees are resilient. Simultaneous shortfalls across two independent income streams suggest sector-wide downturn, not isolated issues.
findings.figures: £1.133m commercial income shortfall, £1.110m planning/development income shortfall
findings.quote: Forecast shortfall in commercial income alongside increase in lease costs... Shortfall in income due to a downturn in development

findings.paper_title: Appendix_1A_2025-26_GF Revenue Monitoring by Variance Q1
findings.headline: Pay award costs of £3.460m unabsorbed structural pressure
findings.detail: Council faces £3.460m high-level cost estimate for pay award at Q1, showing as unabsorbed overspend in corporate budgets. This is a structural cost increase that cannot be managed down within the year.
findings.matters: Unabsorbed pay costs indicate the council is absorbing pay inflation rather than offsetting it, which sets up recurring budget pressure in future years.
findings.quote: High level estimate of pay award cost pressure

findings.paper_title: Appendix_1A_2025-26_GF Revenue Monitoring by Variance Q1
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation demand surge creating £1.546m Q1 exposure
findings.detail: Temporary Accommodation overspend of £0.472m from sharp increase in case numbers and costs per night. Bad debt provision rising by £1.074m in line with growing case numbers. Together this signals a material escalation in housing pressure and credit risk.
findings.matters: A lender assessing cash flow stability needs to know housing obligations are growing faster than budget, and council is building provisions for bad debt on accommodation costs.
findings.figures: £0.472m overspend, £1.074m bad debt provision increase, £1.546m total Q1 exposure
findings.quote: Temporary Accommodation - overspend due to a sharp increase in case numbers and costs per night for accommodation... Bad debt provision - Increase in line with the rising number of Temporary Accommodation cases.

findings.headline: Employment-related whistleblowing complaints represent a notable emerging trend, as overall referrals have grown from 6 to 27 over four years
findings.detail: The council notes an emerging and notable trend in which whistleblowing referrals increasingly concern employment-related matters and decisions, rather than traditional fraud and corruption issues. In parallel, absolute referral volume has increased significantly: from 6 in 2021-22 to 27 in 2024-25.
findings.matters: A shift toward employment complaints could signal emerging management, culture, or conduct concerns within the council that may affect organizational stability and financial resilience.
findings.quote: A notable emerging trend is the growing proportion of referrals concerning employment-related matters and decisions.

findings.headline: Internal Audit team lacks capacity to conclude investigations within the standard six-month timeframe
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies a resource constraint in its Internal Audit, Investigations and Risk Management team that prevents whistleblowing investigations from being completed within six months. The report does not specify typical resolution times, but flags resourcing as the limiting factor.
findings.matters: Timely investigation of fraud and corruption allegations is fundamental to the council's governance and internal control environment. Delayed investigations increase the risk of misconduct going undetected or unresolved.
findings.figures: 5 of 8 new referrals (62.5%) remained open as of July 2025; 16 referrals from previous reporting period required ongoing attention
findings.quote: The resourcing capacity of the IAI team has contributed in not being able to conclude investigations within a six month timeframe.

findings.paper_title: Public Audit and Risk Committee Minutes
findings.headline: Pension fund now approaching 100% funded, reducing future deficit contribution obligations
findings.detail: The Local Government Pension Scheme has improved from 84% funded six to seven years ago to now approaching 100%. Once fully funded, the council will no longer need to make deficit contributions, already factored into financial planning.
findings.matters: Relief from pension deficit contributions will improve annual cash flow and reduce financial obligations
findings.figures: 84% funded six to seven years ago; currently approaching 100%
findings.quote: Six to seven years ago, the fund was approximately 84% funded, requiring significant additional contributions. The current funding level was approaching 100%, and while the Pension Committee had set a cautious upper limit of 120% funding, it would not consider employer contribution holidays unless that threshold was reached.

findings.paper_title: Public Audit and Risk Committee Minutes
findings.headline: New financial system moving to build phase with implementation risks identified
findings.detail: The council is implementing a new financial system consolidating general ledger, debtors, and creditors functions, moving from planning to build phase. The system will provide governance and efficiency benefits, but risks remain until successful implementation.
findings.matters: System implementation failures or control gaps could disrupt financial management, cash control, and reporting accuracy
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: The Committee was also briefed on the implementation of a new financial system, which had moved from the planning phase into the build phase. The system would consolidate general ledger, debtors, and creditors functions, offering efficiencies and governance benefits. However, risks remained until successful implementation.

findings.paper_title: Public Audit and Risk Committee Minutes
findings.headline: PFI contract expiry requires clarity on handover conditions and asset registers
findings.detail: The council has identified the need for clarity in PFI contract documentation as contracts expire, including handover conditions and asset registers. Resources are being secured to appoint a permanent lead to coordinate PFI work across departments.
findings.matters: Unclear PFI handover terms could create unexpected costs, disputes, or loss of control of assets at contract expiry
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: the expiry of PFI contracts was raised and the need for clarity in contract documentation, including handover conditions and asset registers was emphasised. It was confirmed that relevant services were managing this, and resources were being secured to appoint a permanent lead to support and coordinate PFI-related work across departments.

findings.paper_title: Public Audit and Risk Committee Minutes
findings.headline: School's deficit identified as longstanding governance concern requiring active management
findings.detail: The Annual Governance Statement identifies the school's deficit as a longstanding concern, alongside corporate governance issues, with both being actively managed. The specific scale of the deficit is not detailed.
findings.matters: Budget deficits indicate ongoing service pressures and potential draw on general fund reserves
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: Longstanding concerns such as the corporate governance review and the school's deficit were being actively managed.

findings.paper_title: Public Audit and Risk Committee Minutes
findings.headline: Council's partial VAT exemption status poses financial risk if reclaim threshold exceeded
findings.detail: The council's partial VAT exemption creates a financial risk if the reclaim threshold is exceeded. This has been identified as a new governance concern in the Annual Governance Statement, and officers require training to manage the risk.
findings.matters: Exceeding the VAT reclaim threshold could result in unexpected financial loss, indicating a compliance and control gap
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: the council's partial VAT exemption status, where exceeding the reclaim threshold posed a financial risk. Officers required training to manage the risk.

findings.paper_title: 24-25 Internal Audit Annual Report- Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Update Audit and Risk Committee (despatch)
findings.headline: Taranto, a key IT application, received limited assurance with two high priority findings
findings.detail: The audit of Taranto, a critical IT system used across the council, found limited assurance in access controls and rights management, and in business continuity arrangements.
findings.matters: A key IT system with weak access controls or business continuity plans could affect operational resilience, data integrity, and the council's ability to process critical functions.
findings.figures: 2 high priority findings
findings.quote: Completed - Limited assurance. High priority recommendations are included in Appendix 2.

findings.paper_title: 24-25 Internal Audit Annual Report- Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Update Audit and Risk Committee (despatch)
findings.headline: Sundry suppliers financial system received limited assurance with high priority findings
findings.detail: The audit of the council's key financial system for sundry suppliers processing found limited assurance, indicating control weaknesses in how the council processes and authorizes payments to this category of supplier.
findings.matters: Weak controls in a financial system could mean expenditure is not properly authorized or approved, creating risk of fraud, error, or unbudgeted spending.
findings.figures: Limited assurance with high priority findings
findings.quote: Complete - Limited assurance. High priority recommendations are included at Appendix 2.

findings.paper_title: 24-25 Internal Audit Annual Report- Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Update Audit and Risk Committee (despatch)
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation audit found limited assurance with high priority findings
findings.detail: The audit of the council's temporary accommodation function, which assesses processes for monitoring duration, quality and cost, returned limited assurance. High priority recommendations were raised, indicating material control weaknesses in this significant cost area.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a rapidly growing cost for councils; weak controls over duration and cost means spending forecasts may be unreliable and costs could escalate unpredictably.
findings.figures: Limited assurance with high priority findings
findings.quote: Limited assurance – high priority recommendations are included at Appendix 2.

findings.paper_title: 24-25 Internal Audit Annual Report- Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Update Audit and Risk Committee (despatch)
findings.headline: Wenlake Tenant Management Organisation received a 'No assurance' rating with six high priority findings
findings.detail: Wenlake TMO, a council-controlled housing entity, failed an establishment review assessing governance mechanisms and financial practices. No assurance is the worst possible audit rating. Six high priority findings indicate material control failures across the TMO's operations.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that council-controlled entities can maintain basic financial and governance controls; this rating suggests serious failures in one of the council's key housing entities.
findings.figures: Wenlake TMO: 6 high priority findings, No assurance rating
findings.quote: Completed - No assurance. High priority recommendations are included in Appendix 2.

findings.headline: High-priority audit findings in Affordable Workspace Provider arrangements
findings.detail: Substantial audit review of Affordable Workspace Provider generated high-priority recommendations reported to Committee in January 2025. Follow-up in Q1 25/26 showed good progress on implementing these recommendations.
findings.matters: High-priority audit findings in council service arrangements warrant monitoring to ensure governance and financial risks are being properly managed.

findings.quote: In the 2024/25 year to date, Internal Audit has been able to respond to emerging risks, with two substantial additional reviews (in relation to 1) New Build Programme – Payments to Contractors and 2) Affordable Workspace Provider) completed in summer 2024 as outlined in Appendix 1 of this report. High priority recommendations in relation to these areas were reported to the Committee in January 2025. findings.detail: Internal Audit conducted a substantial review of New Build Programme payments to contractors, resulting in high-priority recommendations reported to Committee in January 2025. findings.matters: Control findings in council capital programs directly affect financial risk; demonstrable progress on remediation indicates management's responsiveness to audit recommendations.
