findings.paper_title: 24-25 Internal Audit Annual Report - Appendix 3 - Follow Up Outcomes Audit and Risk Committee (despatch)
findings.headline: Critical social care system (LiquidLogic) follow-up work has not yet commenced
findings.detail: LiquidLogic is a key IT application supporting adult social care. It was originally rated with limited assurance, but follow-up activity has not yet begun and is not planned to start until Q1 2025/26, meaning verification of whether control weaknesses were remedied is delayed.
findings.matters: Delayed follow-up on a critical social care system means the council has not yet verified that control weaknesses are being addressed, and social care is a material spend area for councils facing increasing demand.
findings.figures: Follow-up scheduled Q1 2025/26 onwards
findings.quote: Initial follow up activity will commence in Q1 2025/26, as target completion dates pass.

findings.paper_title: 24-25 Internal Audit Annual Report - Appendix 3 - Follow Up Outcomes Audit and Risk Committee (despatch)
findings.headline: Audit recommendation implementation delays have been escalated to Corporate Directors
findings.detail: The council's audit follow-up process explicitly documents that delays in implementing recommendations and lack of engagement with follow-up requests have been escalated to senior management, indicating that some directorates are not implementing agreed audit actions within planned timeframes.
findings.matters: Escalation of implementation delays to Corporate Directors suggests execution challenges or resource constraints in implementing control improvements across the council, which may indicate broader governance or capacity issues.
findings.figures: None quantified
findings.quote: Where necessary, delays in implementation of recommendations and lack of engagement with follow up requests have been escalated to Corporate Directors.

findings.paper_title: 24-25 Internal Audit Annual Report - Appendix 3 - Follow Up Outcomes Audit and Risk Committee (despatch)
findings.headline: Multiple housing audits required extended follow-up beyond initial investigation
findings.detail: Three housing-related audits needed extended follow-up work: NEC housing platform, TMO monitoring arrangements, and new homes contractor resilience. The fact that these audits were escalated to extended follow-up suggests the initial audits identified control gaps that required deeper investigation than expected.
findings.matters: Housing is a major council service area and revenue driver. The need for extended follow-ups suggests initial audits uncovered control weaknesses in housing oversight, procurement, and systems management that required additional investigation.
findings.figures: 3 audits (R22-2, HN22-3, HN23-1) requiring extended follow-up
findings.quote: Extended follow up outcomes are included in Appendix 1.

findings.paper_title: 24-25 Internal Audit Annual Report - Appendix 3 - Follow Up Outcomes Audit and Risk Committee (despatch)
findings.headline: Safety governance audits rated with no assurance remain in ongoing follow-up activity
findings.detail: Two safety-critical functions — landlord duty of care (lifts) and asbestos governance — were originally rated with no assurance. Both show some implementation of audit actions but both remain in active follow-up, meaning the identified control weaknesses have not been fully resolved.
findings.matters: Unresolved safety governance in housing creates ongoing liability exposure for the council and indicates potential control weaknesses in the landlord function that affect both tenants and the council's risk profile.
findings.figures: 2 audits with 'No assurance' original rating still in follow-up
findings.quote: Good implementation of audit actions. Further follow up activity is in progress.

findings.paper_title: LBI Risk Management Strategy Draft ARC
findings.headline: VAT partial exemption breaches identified as active governance risk
findings.detail: The council's governance risks include VAT partial exemption breaches alongside expiring PFI contracts and other regulatory compliance challenges. The phrasing suggests this is an existing issue being managed rather than a hypothetical risk.
findings.matters: VAT compliance breaches can result in substantial tax liabilities and clawback of previously claimed relief, directly affecting council finances.
findings.figures: none provided
findings.quote: Challenges include VAT partial exemption breaches, expiring PFI contracts, and compliance with new regulatory requirements.

findings.paper_title: LBI Risk Management Strategy Draft ARC
findings.headline: Section 114 notice risk explicitly flagged as a financial outcome
findings.detail: The council has identified in its strategic risk register that severe financial pressures - including funding constraints, capital investment needs for housing and decarbonisation, increasing social care costs, and historic debt obligations - could threaten financial sustainability to the point of triggering a Section 114 notice (the council equivalent of insolvency).
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's own management believes there is material insolvency risk. A Section 114 notice means the council cannot spend money except on statutory duties.
findings.figures: none provided
findings.quote: Severe financial pressures, including funding constraints across all missions, capital investment needs for housing and decarbonisation, increasing social care costs, and historic debt obligations, threaten financial sustainability and heighten the risk of issuing a Section 114 notice.

findings.paper_title: 24-25 Internal Audit Annual Report - Appendix 2 - High priority recommendations Audit and Risk Committee (despatch)
findings.headline: Two school establishment reviews found multiple high-priority governance and financial management weaknesses
findings.detail: Kate Greenaway and Prior Weston schools each identified three high-priority findings in governance, financial management, and income/banking areas, affecting the council's oversight of school operations.
findings.matters: Schools are material service budgets; governance and financial control weaknesses affect the council's ability to manage spend and ensure proper use of public funds.
findings.figures: Three high-priority findings in Kate Greenaway; three high-priority findings in Prior Weston
findings.quote: Governance and financial management; Income charging and banking

findings.headline: 10-year borrowing rates ranged from 4.52% to 5.71%, creating material cost uncertainty
findings.detail: PWLB 10-year certainty rate moved from 4.80% at period start to 5.42% at period end. The full range of available 10-year rates was 4.52% to 5.71%. This 119 basis point spread means capital projects budgeted at one rate could see materially higher costs if rates move during execution.
findings.matters: The council's large capital programme assumes certain borrowing costs. Interest rate volatility means actual debt service costs could be significantly higher than budgeted, particularly given the council's decision to defer borrowing.
findings.figures: 10-year PWLB range 4.52% to 5.71%; start rate 4.80%; end rate 5.42%; weighted average on new borrowing 4.54%
findings.quote: The PWLB certainty rate for 10-year maturity loans was 4.80% at the beginning of the period and 5.42% at the end. The lowest available 10-year maturity rate was 4.52% and the highest was 5.71%.

findings.headline: Council borrowed only £95m of planned £178m, deferring £83m decision to time interest rate movements
findings.detail: The council planned to borrow £178.074m to reduce interest rate risk but only borrowed £95m because higher-than-expected cash balances and higher-than-expected rates at year-end made the council decide 'it was more prudent to wait for a better opportunity'. This shows the council is attempting to time the interest rate market.
findings.matters: If rate forecasts prove wrong and rates rise rather than fall, the council will be forced to borrow £83m+ at higher rates than currently available, materially increasing future debt service costs and straining the budget.
findings.figures: Planned borrowing £178.074m; actual borrowing £95m; deferrred £83.074m (47% shortfall)
findings.quote: With a large capital programme to finance, the Council set out to externally borrow £178.074m throughout 2024/25 to take advantage of a dip in interest rates and reduce interest rate risk. The Council only borrowed £95m (including replacement loan) as higher than expected cash balances and higher than expected rates towards the end of the financial year meant that it was more prudent to wait for a better opportunity.

findings.headline: Capital financing requirement growing 19% over two years from £1035m to £1231m
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement is projected to grow from £1035.093m in 2024/25 to £1231.790m by 2026/27. Combined with an under-borrowing strategy and falling investment income, this growth will either require substantially more external borrowing or rapid depletion of reserves.
findings.matters: Large and growing capital financing needs combined with the under-borrowing strategy and non-repeatable investment income creates pressure on liquidity and may force the council to borrow at unfavourable rates.
findings.quote: The Council has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme and an estimated borrowing requirement as determined by the Liability Benchmark which also considers usable reserves and working capital.

findings.headline: Investment income windfall of £5.1m against £1.75m budget explicitly stated as non-repeatable
findings.detail: The council earned £5.1m in investment income versus a budgeted £1.75m, driven by unexpectedly high short-term rates and larger than expected cash balances. The paper explicitly warns this is a one-off: 'As short term interest rates reduce alongside cash balances this windfall is unlikely to be repeated in future years.'
findings.matters: If future budgets or service sustainability plans depend on achieving this investment income level, they will fail. Forecasters have been over-optimistic about rates and must plan on significantly lower investment returns.
findings.figures: £5.1m actual vs £1.75m budget; 4.94% return vs 4% budget; income overachievement of £3.35m
findings.quote: The Council earned Investment income of £5.1m for the period, this is significantly more than the budget of £1.75m due to both interest rates remaining higher than expected for longer and larger than expected cash balances.

findings.headline: Under-borrowing strategy creates refinancing risk if reserves are depleted or rates rise
findings.detail: The council is deliberately under-borrowed, using cash reserves to fund capital expenditure instead of external loans. This saves interest costs but creates significant risks. The council explicitly lists five risks: inability to finance future capital projects, forced emergency borrowing at higher rates, reduced liquidity and inability to meet payments, foregone returns, and financial shocks from unexpected emergencies due to reserve reliance.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether the council can fund its capital programme and meet obligations if forced to borrow unexpectedly at higher rates or if reserves are drawn down faster than planned.
findings.figures: External borrowing £408.876m; Capital Financing Requirement £1035.093m; internal over-borrowing £522.967m
findings.quote: The Council has an under borrowed position. This has provided significant savings by minimising interest expenses and utilising cash balances to fund the capital programme in the short term, rather than taking out long term loans. This does however present a refinancing risk if rates were to increase significantly.

findings.headline: Market and inflation pressures on pension fund liabilities are increasing faster than assets recover
findings.detail: Falls in asset values and persistent inflation both present high-risk scenarios (rating 15 inherent for each). Falling asset values increase liability valuations; inflation increases the present value of future benefit obligations. Both mitigated to 10. The fund has a diversified strategy with inflation-linked investments and is reviewing natural capital allocation.
findings.matters: Rising pension liabilities require higher employer contributions. Funding shortfalls affect the council's financial capacity and may force either service cuts or higher council tax.
findings.figures: Risk ratings 15 (both scenarios, inherent) reduced to 10 (mitigated); financial impact £100K-£500K per scenario
findings.quote: Reduction in asset market values; increase value of liabilities. Discount rate falls will increase liability valuations.

findings.headline: External payroll providers pose risk of late pension statements and statutory returns
findings.detail: External payroll providers' ineffective planning may delay pension statements and government statutory returns. Risk is rated 15 (inherent, mitigated to 9). Mitigation includes iConnect deployment and late payment penalties for non-compliance by November 2025.
findings.matters: Late statutory returns create regulatory exposure. The council is enforcing late payment penalties against providers, signalling tension in these critical supplier relationships.
findings.figures: Risk rating 15 (inherent) reduced to 9 (mitigated); target Nov-25
findings.quote: The late provision of payroll reports (External Payroll Providers). Ineffective planning

findings.headline: Pension benefit calculations may be inaccurate due to software design fault in the pensions increase application
findings.detail: A software design fault in how pension increases are applied requires training and early engagement with suppliers for a solution. This is rated high risk (15 inherent, mitigated to 12). The payroll manager must provide test data once Treasury publishes pension increase rates, with target resolution by November 2025.
findings.matters: Inaccurate pension benefit calculations create member complaints, potential compensation liability, and reputational damage to the council.
findings.figures: Risk rating 15 (inherent) reduced to 12 (mitigated); target Nov-25
findings.quote: Failure to apply correct Pensions Increase (Corporate Payroll). Software design fault/training required

findings.headline: Manual payroll data processing will continue past December 2025 due to iConnect tool implementation delays
findings.detail: The iConnect tool for importing monthly payroll data to the pensions database is delayed due to validation errors. The council is continuing manual processes, increasing error risk. The mitigation plan involves training from Heywood and deployment of a consultant-assisted solution by December 2025. This is a high-risk item (inherent 15, mitigated 12).
findings.matters: Manual data entry increases the risk of contribution calculation errors, which could trigger member complaints and regulatory action. System delays extend operational inefficiency.
findings.figures: Risk rating 15 (inherent) reduced to 12 (mitigated); target Dec-25
findings.quote: Continuation of manual processes to capture payroll data, increase risk of error as new system not being deployed optimally to achieve efficiencies.

findings.headline: Pension dashboard connection deadline has passed with no confirmation of compliance
findings.detail: Failure to connect to the pensions dashboard by the August 2025 regulatory deadline could trigger fines from the Pensions Regulator. The risk remains rated 8/10 after mitigation as of May 2025, with the council procuring an ISP provider and working with IT and governance teams. The document does not confirm whether the August deadline was met.
findings.matters: Pensions Regulator fines represent a direct cost; non-compliance also signals governance weakness to external stakeholders.
findings.figures: Risk rating 10 (inherent) reduced to 8 (mitigated); target Aug-25
findings.quote: Failure to connect to Pensions dashboard Ineffective planning/poor management. Reputational damage and fines from the Pensions Regulator

findings.headline: Pension payroll reports are heavily dependent on a single external consultant, creating a knowledge gap
findings.detail: The council acknowledges 'far too much dependency on consultant to write all reports' for pension payroll, creating risk of late statutory returns and complaints. The Service Director has committed to building internal training capacity in reporting by September 2025. This is rated high risk (inherent 15, mitigated 9).
findings.matters: Late pension statements and statutory returns damage the council's regulatory standing and create audit risk. Loss of the consultant could cause service disruption until internal capacity is built.
findings.figures: Risk score 15 (inherent) reduced to 9 (mitigated); target Sep-25 for training commitment
findings.quote: Lack of knowledge sharing and far too much dependency on consultant to write all reports.

findings.headline: McCloud age discrimination remedy will increase employer pension costs
findings.detail: The council faces increased employer contributions to remedy unlawful age discrimination identified by the McCloud judgement. The register shows an inherent risk score of 15 (high impact, high likelihood), and the council is exercising discretion to defer remediation for a further year beyond the August 2025 deadline. The exact cost is not quantified in the register.
findings.matters: Pension contributions are a direct cost to the council's budget. Deferred remediation creates a liability cliff when it must be addressed, which affects the council's financial planning.
findings.figures: Risk rating 15 (inherent) reduced to 12 (mitigated); target remediation date Aug-25, deferred further
findings.quote: Remedies in relation to the Mccloud judgement Unlawful age discrimination. Increased employer costs.

findings.paper_title: 2025 Draft Summary Islington Pension Fund Annual Report (revised PC 28-8-25)
findings.headline: LGPS super-pooling reform from March 2026 will transfer all assets to LCIV and impose new governance requirements on pension committee members.
findings.detail: The Government's LGPS Fit for Future reform requires all London boroughs' assets to transfer to the London Collective Investment Vehicle (LCIV) from March 2026. This includes listed and unlisted assets. In addition, pension committee members must meet new mandatory knowledge and skills standards, and administering authorities must publish governance and training strategies.
findings.matters: A major asset transfer is a material operational risk, including potential service disruption, cost changes, and governance transitions. The council must ensure committee members have adequate skills and training, or face regulatory pressure. This is a hard deadline for March 2026 execution.
findings.figures: Transfer date: March 2026; About 50% of Islington's equity assets already pooled via LCIV (53.1% of whole fund under LCIV oversight as of March 2025)
findings.quote: All listed and unlisted assets will transfer to the management of LCIV from March 2026. Pension committee members must meet new knowledge and skills standards, and authorities must publish governance and training strategies.

findings.paper_title: 2025 Draft Summary Islington Pension Fund Annual Report (revised PC 28-8-25)
findings.headline: Pension administration performance below KPI targets on critical processes, indicating potential staffing or process constraints.
findings.detail: Multiple key pension administration processes are running 8–16 percentage points below 90% KPI targets. Transfer-in quotations achieved 74% (target 90%), pension estimates 80% (target 90%), preserved benefit calculations 76% (target 90%), and retirement benefits 82% (target 90%). Despite a 15% increase in total cases processed, performance has not kept pace with demand.
findings.matters: Underperformance in administration can lead to member complaints, regulatory scrutiny from the Pensions Regulator, and damage to the council's governance reputation. It may also signal that the fund administration team lacks resources to handle growing complexity or volume.
findings.figures: Transfer-in quotations 74% vs 90% target; Pension estimates 80% vs 90% target; Preserved benefit calculations 76% vs 90% target; Retirement benefits 82% vs 90% target; Total cases up 15% (3,444 processed)
findings.quote: The table below gives the data for the average performance for the year to 31 March 2025, in respect of the key processes. [Target days, % Achieved within target days, Actual average days showing multiple processes below targets]

findings.paper_title: 2025 Draft Summary Islington Pension Fund Annual Report (revised PC 28-8-25)
findings.headline: 2025 triennial actuarial valuation in progress; employer contribution rates reset April 2026, with outcomes uncertain; fund was 96% funded with £79m deficit at March 2022.
findings.detail: The 2022 valuation set the current 18.4% primary employer contribution rate plus variable secondary contributions (averaging £5.1m annually). A new valuation dated 31 March 2025 is now progressing and will determine new rates effective April 2026. The fund's funding position has improved somewhat (assets grew to £2.03bn, though this reflects market recovery and assumption changes), but the exact impact on rates is unknown.
findings.matters: Employer contribution rates are a fixed cost the council must budget for. Changes in April 2026 could increase the council's pension obligations substantially, reducing budget flexibility. The lender needs to anticipate this moving to the new rate in 2026/27 budgets.
findings.figures: Current: 18.4% primary rate + secondary contributions averaging £5.1m/annum; Fund 96% funded March 2022 (£1,787m assets, £1,866m liabilities, £79m deficit); 16-year recovery period
findings.quote: The next triennial actuarial valuation of the Fund is progressing as at 31 March 2025. Based on the results of this valuation, the contribution rates payable by the individual employers will be revised with effect from 1 April 2026.

findings.paper_title: 2025 Draft Summary Islington Pension Fund Annual Report (revised PC 28-8-25)
findings.headline: Fund runs a cash deficit on current contributions: £81.2m income vs £109.9m expenditure (excluding investment returns), requiring reliance on investment income and employer contributions.
findings.detail: The fund received £81.2m in contributions (excluding investment income) against £109.9m in expenditure during 2024/25. This means the fund is cash-negative on a contribution basis and depends on investment returns and employer top-ups to meet pension payments. This is a structural feature of an ageing fund but signals reduced buffer.
findings.matters: A cash-negative position means the council must make contributions not just to build the fund but to cover the annual shortfall. Combined with rising membership age, this increases the likelihood of higher contribution rate demands at the next valuation.
findings.figures: Income (excl. investment) £81.2m vs Expenditure £109.9m (2024/25); shortfall £28.7m
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2025, £81.2million income (excluding investment income) was received against an expenditure of £109.9 million. The other drivers apart from pension payments were leavers' transfer and lump sum payments.

findings.paper_title: 2025 Draft Summary Islington Pension Fund Annual Report (revised PC 28-8-25)
findings.headline: Pension payments increased 10% to £66.4m, driven by inflation-linked increases of 6.7%, representing a growing annual cost.
findings.detail: Year-on-year pension payments rose from £60.4m to £66.4m, primarily due to the 6.7% annual pension increase applied in the year. Pensions are inflation-linked, meaning the council faces ongoing pressure from higher pension costs as inflation remains elevated relative to pre-pandemic norms.
findings.matters: Pension payment inflation is a fixed cost that grows automatically each year based on CPI. A lender or finance director needs to know this is a structural cost pressure the council cannot easily control.
findings.figures: Pensions paid £66.4m (2024/25) vs £60.4m (2023/24); 6.7% annual pension increase applied
findings.quote: Pensions paid totalled £66.4million compared to £60.4million in 2023/24. The increase was mainly due to the annual pension increase of 6.7%.

findings.paper_title: 2025 Draft Summary Islington Pension Fund Annual Report (revised PC 28-8-25)
findings.headline: Membership profile is ageing: pensioners and deferred members now outnumber active employees.
findings.detail: As of March 2025, the fund has 7,216 pensioners, 7,050 active employees, and 8,636 deferred members. The trend since 2015 shows pensioners growing from 5,951 to 7,216 and deferred members from 8,879 to 8,636, while active employee growth has stalled (8,799 to 7,050). This shifting ratio reduces the base of contributors relative to beneficiaries.
findings.matters: An ageing membership profile increases the council's long-term pension funding pressure, as fewer active employees support more retirees. This affects both contribution rates and the sustainability of the fund.
findings.figures: Pensioners 7,216 (2025) vs 5,951 (2015); Active employees 7,050 (2025) vs 8,799 (2015); Deferred members 8,636 (2025) vs 8,879 (2015)
findings.quote: The scheme membership continues to grow year on year. Deferred members and pensioners are increasing compared to active employees.
